## What an L2 detail specification could adopt, adapt, or must argue against

- **The subject of the row, tested at the object: an on-task, cross-validated, head-to-head measurement of
  a GENERATIVE and a DISCRIMINATIVE model family for the chord decision.** The candidacy row's reason —
  *"the shape of the choice an L2 detail specification makes"* — is confirmed: the paper compares exactly
  the two families a specification deciding DP-P / DP16 must choose between or combine, on chord labels,
  under a protocol the record's own D-270 shares in shape (folds grouped by whole piece). **What the
  measurement says, read with its unprinted spread in mind:** at the matched single-Gaussian emission the
  CRF is below the model-discriminant HMM (34.7 against 37.1 rotated, 29.9 against 39.7 unrotated); the
  best CRF cell (CRF-D, 45.3) is below the best HMM cell (HMM-MD, 48.8); the authors' conclusion is that
  the CRF *"comes very close… while using a factor of 40 fewer model parameters"*. **The paper does not
  decide the family question; it measures one data size (twenty songs) and finds the generative model still
  ahead there.** This is the shape row 13's general result — as the progress record's item (e) states it
  (finding (3) of row 13's extract, which this sitting did not open): the discriminative fit has the lower
  asymptote but needs more data to reach it, so the two orderings cross — predicts for a small training
  set. **This paper is a held, on-task measurement consistent with the small-data half of that result;
  whether any OTHER held paper in the slice measures the two families head to head on the chord decision
  was NOT checked, and no superlative is asserted. It is NOT a test of the crossover: one data size cannot
  locate a crossing, and the paper does not claim to.** A detail specification arguing for D-525's staged fit
  (counted tables plus a small discriminatively-fitted weight vector) against a fully discriminative fit of
  the kind rows 10, 12 and 14 instantiate would cite this paper for the on-task datum, with the domain bound
  and the absent uncertainty stated. **Nothing about the family choice is settled by it.**
- **Adapt (the paper's stated ground for the discriminative family, on-task).** §3.2's argument — that a
  conditional model *"frees the recogniser from needing to enforce any particular model P(X) of the data,
  and thus it is no longer necessary for the components of the observation vectors to be conditionally
  independent"* — is row 12's claim restated by a music paper and then INSTANTIATED: CRF-DG feeds two
  overlapping descriptions of the same PCP vector into one score. **The measured instance is mixed:** CRF-DG
  is above CRF-D rotated (39.9 against 39.5) and below it unrotated (42.4 against 45.3). For L2, whose
  score combines several evidence sources over the same notes (§S4(c)'s ten factors, not independent of
  one another), the claim belongs to row 12's paper, whose extract this sitting did not open (the progress
  record's table names that extract's findings (3), (4), (5), (6), (7) and (15) as the claims a
  specification would cite, without saying which is this one); what this row adds is that an on-task
  attempt to exploit it bought nothing separable from the unprinted spread. Cited to row 12 for the claim
  and to this paper for the instance.
- **A datum for DP-B / §S4(b) and for D-526, and it is MEASURED — with the tonality supplied as an
  oracle.** The rotated condition expresses every chord relative to a given global key (features and
  labels both transposed to C), which is the scale-degree-valued chord axis D-526 states in the state
  space, here reached by relabelling — and it is *tonality first, then chord* in its crudest form, with
  the *first* step taken as known and not decided by the system *(★ CORRECTED 2026-09-19, ON THE USER'S
  SECOND RULING; former wording, preserved (#12): "the *first* step done by hand" — the page names no source
  for the key)*. **The measured effect of key-relative against absolute representation
  is of MIXED SIGN:** for the HMMs, within 4.6 points either way (the 24-Gaussian row aside), the sign
  flipping with the number of Gaussians; for CRF-G, +4.8 for key-relative; for CRF-D, −5.8; for CRF-DG,
  −2.5. **So with a PERFECT key, relabelling chords by degree did not reliably help this system on this
  music, and the authors say the pattern *"warrants further investigation"*.** This is another
  published instance of the root-invariance idea beside the three row 18's extract names (rows 3 and 20,
  which pool a transition table and augment by key shift, and row 18 itself, which pools the emission by
  rotation and measures a gain in one direction); **here the effect is measured with MIXED sign.** Whether
  any row read after row 18 measures a key-relative encoding was not checked, and no count and no
  superlative is asserted. It bears on DP-B's rival (tonality first) only as a
  datum about what a supplied key buys a downstream chord model, not on DP-B's ground (Rocher's ablation
  measures a decided key, not a given one). Routed to L2's detail specification beside D-526 and to the
  findings surface's DP-B block as a domain-bounded datum; no verdict.
- **Must argue against (the fixed frame grid).** Every model here decides one label per 92 ms frame —
  the *"before (every fixed grid)"* member of DP-C's candidate list. Its boundaries are frame edges, not
  L1's change points, so its figures are for a decision on a different candidate set from L2's and are not
  comparable with any figure the record publishes. Same shape as row 18 (its extract's own
  must-argue-against item on the 100 ms grid, read at the object).
- **Must argue against (one best path, no rivals).** The single Viterbi path is the whole output, for the
  CRFs too, although an exact per-frame marginal exists for that model. The L2 charter publishes rivals
  with their mass. Another instance beside the ones row 18's extract names (rows 11, 19, 20 and 18 itself;
  no count is asserted), and — beside row 16's finding (5), the per-span marginal as a confidence route, as
  the hundred-and-fifty-third entry and the progress record's table state it — a case of a model that
  could publish a marginal exactly and does not.
- **Must argue against (a per-frame linear-chain shape, not a segmental one).** Both families here are
  the base case item (g) of the progress record names for row 12: labels on a fixed chain, segments as runs
  of equal labels, no segment or length variable. What the paper measures is the family choice one level
  below L2's chosen semi-Markov shape (rows 10, 11, 19); the transfer of its ordering to a segmental score
  is not established by it and is not claimed by it.
- **Not transferable, recorded so it is not carried across domains (the Dirichlet emission).** The
  Dirichlet is chosen because a normalised chroma vector lies on the simplex — an audio-feature argument.
  L2's emission is per tone by category over given notes (D-527), and no normalised chroma exists at L0.
  The paper's strongest result is therefore about a feature this project does not have.
- **A datum for the candidate-admission boundary condition (the L2 charter's second fixed clause).** The
  vocabulary was cut from sevenths to triads because *"the data set was insufficient to estimate so many
  models properly"*, and 24 of the 48 admitted triads never occur in the labels. A published instance of an
  admission rule set by fitting capacity rather than by the music — the opposite of what the charter
  requires the rule to defend — routed to L2's detail specification where the admission rule and its
  defense live.
- **Corroboration, not adoption (the protocol).** The paper's thesis that cross-validation is *"the only
  fair way to compare different models"*, with folds of whole songs, agrees with the record's D-270
  (five-fold, grouped by ground-truth file) and D-097. It is a published statement of the record's own
  protocol from the audio field in 2007; nothing is adopted from it, and it adds no ground the record
  lacks.

- **Adapt — the candidate-admission rule, stated explicitly.** The L2 charter fixes that *"the rule that
  admits a candidate to the search is part of this layer's specification and carries its own defense"*
  (`FRAMEWORK.md` line 421–424, read this session). This paper is a published, on-repertoire instance of
  such a rule written out in full: three harmonic rules and four melodic rules, with the seven elaboration
  types defined by approach, departure and metric position, and with the authors' own statement that the
  rules are not universally agreed and are over-fitted to chorales. A specification writing L2's admission
  rule for this repertoire would cite this paper's §3 as the nearest published enumeration of what such a
  rule must say, and would have to argue where it differs — in particular on Harmonic Rule 2 (no syncopated
  harmonic rhythm), which is a HARD constraint on segmentation against meter, and on Harmonic Rule 3's
  chord vocabulary. Cited to §3; the judgment that it is the nearest published enumeration is this reader's
  and is bounded by what this pass has read.
- **Adapt — the enumeration as the shape of L2's search over a bounded window.** The paper's Stage 2 is an
  exhaustive joint search over sub-segmentation × non-chord-tone combination × chord identity, with
  pruning rules (Steps 5–8) that discard illegal, incomplete-where-complete-exists, redundant and subsumed
  readings. That is the search the L2 charter's *"discard a rival before the whole sequence of spans has
  been scored"* clause forbids cutting short — and the paper cuts it short only by legality, never by
  score, which is the one kind of discard the clause does not reach. A specification would cite Steps 1–8
  for the enumeration and Step 7 for the dedup of readings that differ only in a boundary between two
  slices carrying the same chord. What the paper does NOT supply is the score over the survivors; DP-P's
  question is untouched by it.
- **Must argue against — the hard window in Stage 1.** The contextual-window heuristic decides boundaries
  BEFORE the labelling, on notation alone, and those boundaries are never revisited. The paper's own stated
  reason is to *"err on the side of larger segments"* so that the joint enumeration inside a window has
  the context it needs; it acknowledges that a too-small window *"may result in windows that are not
  parsable"*. This is DP-C's *before* candidate at the window level, chosen by the paper for tractability
  — exactly the *"Rival's ground"* DP-C records (*"tractability, and the availability of segment-level
  features"*, line 692) — with DP-C's *with* answer inside each window. A specification carrying DP-C's
  exclusion of *before* would cite this as the hybrid it is, and would have to say why a hard window is or
  is not an instance of the excluded shape; the paper measures nothing about what its windows cost.

## What an L2 detail specification could adopt, adapt, or must argue against

**Nothing in the architecture would be adopted**, and the reason is structural rather than a judgment of
quality: the method classifies each onset slice independently, under a fixed grid, with a context window
of one or two slices on each side supplied as extra input features. It carries **no segment variable, no
boundary variable, no length term, no rival set and no mass**, and it decides no tonality. Against the
worked shapes this slice has collected for the length term, **it adds no new shape and could not**: it is
one level below even row 12's base case, since row 12 at least labels a chain with a transition structure,
while this method's slices are classified independently and a "segment" is only a run of equal labels
after the fact. **The rows are named and no count is asserted.**

**What WOULD carry load in a detail specification is the paper's MEASUREMENTS, and they are of three
kinds.**

1. **The ordering of the chord-tone assignment against the chord identity, measured end to end on this
   project's own repertoire.** This is DP-D's own question. **NO CLAIM IS MADE THAT THIS IS THE ONLY PAPER
   IN THE SLICE THAT MEASURES IT, and the first writing of this file made one:** this side read no other
   row's paper and opened only rows 35's, 57's and 10's extracts, so what the other twenty-eight read rows
   measure is not established here. What IS established is that **this paper measures it**, and that row
   35's extract — the excluded rival's own — records that row 35's paper does not. Finding (3).
2. **A figure for row 57's method**, which row 57's own paper does not report. Finding (4).
3. **How much one slice of context on either side is worth for the chord decision**, on symbolic Bach
   chorales. Finding (5).

**And one boundary statement** an L2 detail specification would have to answer rather than adopt: the
paper's own future-work sentence names *"training and evaluation protocols that permit multiple valid chord
labels per slice"* as **work this group has yet to do** — the paper says *"we will investigate"*, which is a
statement about their own plans and **not** a claim that the field has not built such protocols. Finding (8).

## ★ Findings, routed and not applied

one-author-and-*et al.* shape is not confined to this row in the bibliography, `BIBLIOGRAPHY.md` line 85
(*"Koops et al."*, candidacy row 61, NOT ADMITTED) having it too, though that row has no row in the read
table, so the block's own sentence stands as written.

**(2) ★ THE DOUBT DEFAULT'S OWN QUESTION IS ANSWERED AT THE OBJECT, AND THE ANSWER IS BOTH: THE WORKFLOW
CARRIES A LABELLING METHOD — FOUR OF THEM — AND IS ALSO A TOOL FOR PRODUCING A CORPUS.** The derivation
asks *"does the workflow carry a labelling METHOD, or is it a tool for producing a corpus?"* The paper
carries **four models that each label every chord** (§1 step 2, Figure 2's caption): a rule-based model
(row 57's), a non-chord-tone remover followed by a heuristic labeller, a non-chord-tone remover followed by
a trained labeller, and a trained labeller applied directly to the pitch-class collections; an **unweighted
ensemble vote with a declared tie-break**; and a **human-in-the-loop correction confined to the
non-unanimous slices**, followed by re-training. **Models 1, 2 and 3 are measured in both experiments; the
rule-based Model 4 is measured in Experiment 2 only** — Table 1 carries CA1, CA2 and CA3 and no CA4 —
**so "all four measured twice", which the first writing of this file said, is false at the tables.** **So the L2 placement holds
at the object and the row is not a corpus row** — the corpus half is the workflow's *purpose*, and the
labelling half is its *content*. Row 39's precedent is the opposite outcome (a doubt-default row whose
reading moved it out of the layer its row placed it in); row 16's is the same outcome by a different route
(a doubt-default row answered by what the paper explains rather than measures). **This one is answered by
what the paper MEASURES.** Nothing moves in the derivation; the answer is recorded here and the row's
placement is confirmed rather than corrected.

**(3) ★★ AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO DP-D's GROUND: THE EXCLUDED RIVAL's PIPELINE IS MEASURED END TO END
AGAINST THE NO-DETECTOR PIPELINE, ON THIS PROJECT'S OWN REPERTOIRE, BY THE RIVAL'S OWN AUTHORS — AND IT
MEASURES SLIGHTLY AHEAD. PUT TO THE USER AND APPLIED NOWHERE.**

*What the record says.* DP-D (`FRAMEWORK.md` lines 703–710, read whole this session) and §S6's DP4 (lines
1807–1815, read whole this session) exclude the rival *"an input, from an elaboration detector running
first (published; F .72)"* on this ground: *"its own authors report F .72 with many 'errors' that are
plausible analytical choices, and a first-running detector's mistakes are unrecoverable downstream."*
Row 35's extract — the paper that F .72 comes from — records at its finding (6) that **that paper
advocates the pipeline DP-D excludes and does not build or test it**, and that *"unrecoverable
downstream"* is the record's own reasoning rather than the paper's.

*What this paper does.* It builds that pipeline and the alternative, and measures both on chord labels.
**"NCT-first harmonic analysis"** (Models 1 and 2: remove the non-chord tones, then label) against
**"direct harmonic analysis"** (Model 3: label the pitch-class collection without removing anything) —
the paper's own terms, Figure 2's and Figure 3's captions. On the hand-annotated reserved test set
(Table 2), Model 2 against Model 3 reads **88.6 against 87.7 (SVM, pre-trained)**, **89.8 against 89.3
(SVM, re-trained)**, **88.9±0.3 against 87.9±0.7 (DNN, pre-trained)** and **91.3±0.4 against 90.5±0.3
(DNN, re-trained)** — **NCT-first ahead in all four**, by between 0.5 and 1.0 points. On Experiment 1's
cross-validation against the rule-based model's own output (Table 1), **the sign is MIXED, and the ten

## ★ The placement question, DECIDED AT THE PAPER

The slice-derivation row (line 79) places row 40 in **L2's slice with an L3 bearing**, and says in
terms: *"What in it is L3's the row does not say; noted, not decided."* This is the answer, taken at the
paper and against the two charters read whole this session (`FRAMEWORK.md` §5, L2 at its heading and L3
at its heading, with the boundary contracts).

**The charters, quoted rather than paraphrased.** L2 publishes *"per span, the **tonality** as tonic and
mode"* and *"per span, the **chord** as degree, quality, figure and applied target, read against that
tonality"*. L3 publishes *"the **cadence** at each phrase end, with its type; the **phrase and section
grouping**; the **chord symbol** … the **figured bass**; the **harmonic rhythm**."* The boundary
contract L2 → L3 is forward-only and the contract L3 → L2 is **"Nothing."**

**The answer: the paper's own unit of record straddles the boundary, and it straddles it by
construction rather than by accident.** Its encoding token — *"III-IA3"* — carries, in one string and
in one annotating act, **(1) a local key area, which is L2's tonality per span; (2) a cadence
classification, which is L3's cadence type; and (3) the soprano's chord member at the arrival, which is
a read-off from a chord L2 decides.** The paper's central object, Tables 7 and 8 and the Figure 18
flowchart, is a **conditional distribution over the (key area, cadence type) PAIR given a melodic
fact** — the soprano's scale degree at the arrival and the interval leading into it, both of which are
L0/L1 facts about the notated melody.

**So what in it is L3's is the cadence-type half of every one of its labels, and what in it is L2's is
the local-key-area half — and the paper's finding is precisely about the pair, not about either half.**

**What this does NOT license, stated because the distance is short and the step would be wrong.** It is
**not** a refutation of DP-I / DP9's split (*cues at L1, type at L3*), and this read does not offer it
as one: that split is about where a cadence's TYPE is decided relative to the harmony, and a type read
off a decided harmony at L3 is entirely consistent with a corpus in which the composer chose key and
cadence together. What the paper bears on is **the evidence available to the L2 half** — whether the
tonality decision at a phrase ending can be taken well without the cadence-type question being open at
the same time. **That is a question this paper raises and does not answer**, because it never decides
anything: it records what Bach did, by hand, and tabulates it. **No claim is made here that the
framework's boundary is wrong**, and none should be read into this section.

**One further thing the paper settles about its own placement.** The paper's tonality is read **only at
fermata events**. It encodes nothing about the tonality between phrase endings, and it therefore says
nothing at all about a tonality change away from a cadence. **A reading that took this paper as
evidence FOR DP-E's clause that "a tonality change is located at a harmonic boundary" would be reading
the study's design as its result** — the design presupposes the reading is taken at the cadential
arrival, so it cannot test the clause. That is stated here so a later session does not make the step.

so the stated bound is not the difference of the two printed rates.** Read instead against the

prints "Less then" for "less than"; that is a spelling slip and is recorded only so a later search on
the phrase does not miss it.)*

## ★ FINDING (1) — A CORRECTED STRUCTURAL CLAIM CANDIDATE on DP-O's and DP15's live `[FACT]` text: the three figures do not measure the claim they are attached to

**What the record's sentence does.** At both homes the sentence joins, with the word *"with"*, (a) a
representational claim — *"a recursive grammar represents something a flat sequence cannot — the same
surface chords functioning simultaneously as a tonic phrase in one tonality and a dominant phrase in
another"* — and (b) three measured figures. A reader takes the figures as the measurement of the
claim. **They are not.**

**What is the paper's and what is not.**

- The **illustration** is the paper's, in its own words, at §1 on Figure 1's analysis of *Afternoon in
  Paris*: *"Note that the subsequence Cm⁷ F⁷ B♭△ is both a tonic progression in B♭ major and a dominant
  progression in E♭ major. It forms a dominant phrase in A♭ major together with B♭m⁷ and E♭⁷."*
  **That sentence is about one analysis of one A-part. It is not a claim about what a flat sequence
  can or cannot represent, and nothing in the paper measures it.**
- **Across the eight pages read whole**, the phrase **"something a flat sequence cannot"** does not
  appear in any form, and **no flat sequence model appears at all.** The four models compared at §6.2
  are: a PACFG, a PCFG, randomly generated **trees**, and a right-branching **tree** baseline. **All
  four produce trees.** No HMM, no CRF, no n-gram, no latent-category sequence model and no flat
  tagger occurs in those eight pages, which is the object this claim is made at and the only one.
- The **39.43% comparand is another context-free grammar** over the same rule set, differing from the
  winner in one property only: whether the rule distribution is shared across keys. **So the
  45.95-against-39.43 comparison measures transposition-tying — parameter sharing — and not recursion
  against flatness.**
- The **right-branching baseline** is the only comparand that could be read as "flat", and it is a
  degenerate **tree** with no learned grammar at all, sitting below even the random-tree baseline
  (15.35%). *"under 10%"* is the cost of having no model, not the cost of being a sequence model.

**Why this is structural and not cosmetic.** DP-O's own falsifier, immediately below the sentence, is
*"a tree model beating a matched-capacity **sequence** model on this repertoire's ground truth"*. **DP-O
itself sets up a tree-versus-sequence axis, and then puts on its *for* side three figures that lie on
a different axis entirely.** A reader who arrives at the falsifier from the for-side sentence will
take the 45.95/39.43 pair as partial evidence toward it. It is not evidence toward it at all.

**THE OTHER READING, STATED IN FULL so the user can take it.** The word *"with"* can be read as merely
conjoining two things the paper offers — a representational point it illustrates, and a measured
result it reports — without asserting that the second measures the first. On that reading nothing in
the sentence is false: the illustration is the paper's, the figures are the paper's, the attribution
of the 39.43 comparand is accurate, and the sentence claims no causal link. **What would still be
true under that reading is that the sentence supplies no evidence on DP-O's own axis while appearing
to**, which is a case for adding a clause rather than for striking one.

**WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, and this decides the STOP question.** The commission's §5, **read at the object
this session and quoted whole rather than by its branch (D-643)**, makes a STOP of *"A CORRECTED
structural claim **that moves a design-point verdict**; a derived upgrade the environment cannot fetch
or read; anything requiring an act outside §0's licence; and any point at which the derivation cannot
place a paper."* **DP-O's verdict is NONE CHOSEN — underived: open, and this finding leaves it exactly
there** — if anything it makes the openness better founded. **NO STOP FIRES**, and the ground is the
commission's own words.

*(The progress record's item (b⁶) states the STOP condition as "a corrected structural claim on that
ground is a STOP". That is wider than the commission's text, which requires the correction to MOVE a
verdict. Applied literally, (b⁶)'s wording would have fired a STOP the commission does not order. This
is recorded at Finding (3) below.)*

## ★ FINDING (6) — A RIVAL SHAPE for DP-E that the record's rival list does not hold

**DP-E, quoted from `FRAMEWORK.md` lines 712–714:** *"**CHOSEN: with the chords; a tonality change is
located at a harmonic boundary.** *Rival:* an independent tonality track changing anywhere, which the
output the analysis must produce cannot express."* **Two shapes are recorded: the chosen one and one
rival.**

**This paper's shape is a third.** The key is a component of **every category** (`C = Z₇ × K`), so
every node of the tree — internal nodes included — carries a key. A modulation is the application of a
rewrite function (`MODULATION`, `MODE-CHANGE`, `DOM-PREP` through `μ(x,k)`) **at an internal node**,
and therefore attaches to a **constituent spanning many chords** rather than to a boundary between two
of them. **It is neither "located at a harmonic boundary" nor "an independent track changing
anywhere": it is a tonality attached to a hierarchical constituent.**

**Why it is worth recording rather than dismissing.** DP-E's stated ground for excluding its one rival
is that the required output *cannot express* it. **That ground does not reach this third shape**,
because a key attached to a constituent can be read down to the chords the constituent spans and
written inline exactly as the ground truth writes it. **Whether that makes it a live rival is not
decided here** — it is an addition to the rival record, applied nowhere, and DP-E stays chosen.

## Where this paper sits against the shapes the slice already holds (item (g))

**Row 21 adds NO new shape to the length-term question, and could not.** It carries **no segment
variable, no boundary variable and no length term at all**: its leaves are chords that arrive already
individuated, and a constituent's span is derived from leaf indices after the fact. **It decides
nothing about where one harmony gives way to the next** — that is given to it. Row 12's reason in
another key: it is not a model of segment formation at all.

**Where it DOES add a shape is on the other axis — what follows what.** Against the transition
machinery the slice already holds, it is the first member that answers *what follows what* with a
**recursive constituent structure over the whole sequence** rather than with a Markov or semi-Markov
transition. And it is the first to answer the sparsity problem that machinery has by **parameter
tying** rather than by back-off:

- **`D-533` (LIVE · 2026-07-19 · ratified by user, read at its home this session)** answers sparsity by
  **proportional back-off** — a row's leftover mass divided in proportion to each chord's overall
  frequency.
- **This paper answers it two other ways at once**: **tying the rule distribution across all keys of a
  mode** (§4), and **Dirichlet pseudocounts** in the variational posterior (§3.3).
- **It measures the first and not the second**, and it does not compare either against back-off.

**So three shapes for one problem, and the record holds one.** Recorded as an addition to the rival
record for the transition-table sparsity question; **no candidate against D-533 is raised**, since
tying and back-off are not exclusive.

## What an L2 detail specification could adopt, adapt, or must argue against

**Could ADOPT.**

- **Key-independent parameter tying over a categorical rule distribution.** This is D-526's consequence
  (b) and D-532's reused mechanism, here with a measured comparison behind it (Finding 4).
- **Dirichlet pseudocounts with a mean-field variational posterior** as the smoothing route, beside
  D-533's back-off (item (g) above). **Unmeasured in this paper.**

**Could ADAPT.**

- **The `(scale degree, key)` category type.** It is D-526's chord axis under another name, with the
  tonality carried in the state rather than beside it.
- **A transition term over what-follows-what derived from a grammar**, folded into L2's score rather
  than standing as a layer above it. **That is precisely what DP-O's own sentence points at** —
  *"what chord follows what is inside L2's charter, and a grammar is one way to answer it"*.

**Must ARGUE AGAINST, and this is the decisive half.**

- **The input contract.** A grammar over chord symbols **cannot answer three of L2's four questions**.
  L2's sentence asks *"what is the tonality at each moment, where does each harmony give way to the
  next, which sounding notes belong to the harmony and which elaborate it, and what chord is read over
  each span?"* **This method receives the answers to the second and fourth, has no access to the data
  the third needs, and answers only the first — and it answers that only as a by-product of parsing.**
  Adopting it whole would mean stacking it on top of a committed chord stream, which is the pipeline
  shape §S4(e) excludes and which L3's boundary contract forbids from revising L2.
- **The evaluation axis.** Tree-span precision grades the hierarchy, not the reading. **A model can
  score well on it while getting every chord wrong, because the chords are given.** No figure of this
  paper can be compared with any agreement figure this project uses.
- **The measured pathology of the device it recommends** (Finding 4's counterweight): relative-key
  alternation is the authors' own conjectured explanation of a measured over-use, and the cause they
  name is the sharing itself.

## 2. The input and the repertoire, established at page 1 and at the paper's own data section (e⁷)

**THE INPUT IS MIDI NOTE EVENTS, NOT A SCORE AND NOT CHORD SYMBOLS.** §4.1 (printed p. 16): the musical
data is MIDI files; a note event carries pitch, onset and duration. The author states the cost in his own
words: *"The MIDI format is far from being a close representation of musical surface, or the musical
score… For the present purposes, the representation particularly lacks of information on fermatas –
therefore, aspects of phrasing could not be included into the research."* The available information is
**key signature, metre, note onset and duration, given in beats**; and the format *"only allows one
specified metre"*, so chorales with a metre change are a known problem (B203, B204, B350 are named).

**So row 23's input differs from row 21's and from ours, and in both directions.** Row 21 takes a
chord-symbol sequence; row 23 takes note events; **our own L0 publishes a notated record with spelling,
which row 23's input does not carry** — MIDI pitch is a number, and §3.1 (printed p. 10) says the pc-set
representation *"reduces a chord to an unordered set of chromatic (enharmonically equivalent) pitch
classes"*. **Enharmonic equivalence is asserted by the representation, not inferred.**

**The repertoire is Bach's four-part chorales, and the corpus is the author's own.** §4.2 (printed p. 17):
downloaded from `JSBChorales.net` in the version of 14 April 2005, **521 MIDI files**; files of fewer than
four parts excluded and only the four-part set taken from larger files; B350 excluded as a five-part
chorale; only chorales in the Riemenschneider or Kalmus editions selected; **61 doublets** detected and
excluded. **Table 4.2: 386 pieces, 61 doublets, 201 major, 185 minor**, average length in beats
`26 ≤ 64.21 ≤ 426` and in pc sets under dense segmentation `30 ≤ 95.53 ≤ 882`. Table 4.3 prints the
per-key piece counts.

**★ THERE IS NO HARMONIC GROUND TRUTH IN THIS STUDY AT ALL, AND THAT IS THE LOAD-BEARING BOUND ON
EVERYTHING IT REPORTS.** No Roman numerals, no human harmonic analyses, no annotated corpus. The only
human-decided quantity anywhere in the pipeline is the **key of each piece**, and that is decided by a
rule-based heuristic the author built himself (§4.4), not by an annotator. **So nothing in this paper is
an accuracy against a human analysis**, and none of its figures is commensurable with anything this
project grades under the ruled convention that the only ground truth is the human annotation (**D-294**,
read at the `DECISIONS.md` index row this session and not at its home). *Narrowed deliberately: the claim
is that no figure of this paper is an accuracy against a human harmonic analysis, which is what that

## 7. The findings, each with what it is a candidate for and what bounds it

**Finding (1) — AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO D-533's GROUND, WHICH CURRENTLY CITES A CLASS AND NAMES NO
SOURCE.** D-533 (read whole at `decisions/group_A.md:703-729`, **LIVE**, decided 2026-07-19, ratified by
user) rules that a continuation too rare to have its own stored probability is scored by dividing the
row's leftover in proportion to each chord's overall frequency, and its stated *Why* is that *"it is the
standard construction in published back-off models of sequences (#1)"* — **a class, with no work named.**
Row 23 states the same problem on this project's own repertoire and proposes the same family of remedy:
§6, *"the method has to face the problem of data sparsity as it may happen that input includes pc
sets/sequences which are unknown to the profile… It could for instance successively cut n-grams into
n-1-grams until they are found or can be combined with classical pitch class profiles."* **What bounds
it:** row 23's units are pc SETS, not degree-valued chords, and it proposes back-off over *n*-gram ORDER
rather than over a row's leftover mass. **So it is a candidate addition to the GROUND and not to the
mechanism**, and it does not discharge D-533's missing citation, which would need a work in the back-off
literature itself.

**Finding (2) — AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO D-532's GROUND, ON THE ONE PROPERTY D-532 EXISTS TO RESTORE.**
D-532 (read whole at `decisions/group_A.md:667-701`, **LIVE**, user-ratified) adds a pooling level so the
chord-transition table can express that a secondary dominant resolves to its target, its defect having
been *"verified directly in the table and its cost measured in a checked passage."* Row 23 reports, on 386
Bach chorales, the general property that makes such a distinction real: *"whereas the pairs in the random
corpus tend to be rather symmetric, this property is not shared in the chorale corpus. Important
progressions tend to be directional. This confirms the common intuition of music as a goal-directed
process in a quantitative way."* **What bounds it:** the asymmetry is reported for pc-set pairs against a
random corpus, not for secondary dominants, and the paper names no chord class. **It is evidence that
directionality is measurable in this repertoire, not evidence about D-532's own cell.**

**Finding (3) — AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO DP-D's EXCLUSION GROUND, IN THE AUTHOR'S OWN WORDS AND ON OUR
REPERTOIRE.** DP-D (`FRAMEWORK.md:703-711`, read whole) excludes a first-running elaboration detector, its
ground being the analyst's note, ledger C26, and the 2017 detector's own F .72. **Row 23 BUILT a
first-running reduction — the harmony approximation, R1 — and states its failure in exactly the shape
DP-D's ground asserts:** *"the case of a V6/4 chord which resolves into a V5/3 on the quaver level cannot
be easily and reliably distinguished from an instance of a I–V progression without reference to an
embedding context."* And on the whole class: *"the practice of Bach's chorales shows that there might be
no simple rule-based system which correctly identifies transitory dissonances, neighbour notes and
suspensions and their resolutions correctly."* **What bounds it:** this is an author's statement about his
own heuristic, unquantified — he reports no error rate for R1 — so it corroborates DP-D's ground and
measures nothing.

**Finding (4) — AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO THE L1 CHARTER's AND DP-C's GROUND: A PUBLISHED STATEMENT THAT
THE CHANGE-POINT GRID ALONE CANNOT DISCRIMINATE ELABORATION.** The L2 charter fixes the segmentation as
*"a partition of the working span into harmonic spans whose boundaries are a subset of L1's change
points"* (`FRAMEWORK.md:393-394`), and §4.2's C27 states that the discriminating information lives in the
boundary placement. **Row 23 defines dense segmentation as a grid close to our change-point grid — cut at note
onsets, by its formal definition — and then states its insufficiency directly:** *(★ CORRECTED
2026-09-20 on the user's ruling of that date, recorded in the banner. FORMER WORDING, PRESERVED (#12):
"Row 23 defines dense segmentation as our change-point grid and then states its insufficiency directly:".
See the note at §3(a). The finding's point does not depend on the difference.)* *"this method […] treats all note events equally and there is no distinction between
a semiquaver passing event and a crotchet chord. Thus, this method is useful to investigate the range and
transitions of the whole set of pc sets occurring in a piece, but is inadequate to reveal the similarity
of patterns which just differ slightly, are elaborations of a simpler structure or are rhythmical
variations of each other."* *(★ CORRECTED 2026-09-19 at the second extraction's cross-check, under the
standing rule of handoff entry 198 §7. FORMER WORDING, PRESERVED (#12): the quotation opened "this method
treats all note events equally", closing up silently what the page prints between those words — a
footnote mark and the parenthesis "('dense segmentation')" (printed 10, requested again at the
cross-check). The omission is now marked. No word of the finding moves.)* **What bounds it:** he is arguing for a REDUCTION and against the grid's use as
an analytical unit, where our charter uses the grid as the candidate boundary set for a decision taken
later. **The two are compatible, and the value is that the insufficiency is stated independently, on this
repertoire, by a source the record does not yet cite.**

**Finding (5) — AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO THE GROUND UNDER THE EXOTIC-MODE GRADING CONVENTION, WITH ITS
COUNTERWEIGHT.** `CLAUDE.md` gate block (A) carries the ruled convention that an exotic mode is graded
against its parent collection's minor key rather than against its own tonic triad, on a measured ground.
**No figure of that measurement is restated here — gate block (A) is a CONDITIONALLY-read span of
`CLAUDE.md` and this side did not read it at the object this session (#17f, D-431).** **Row 23
meets the same problem and decides it the same way, on the same repertoire, for a stated reason that is
NOT ours:** §4.4, *"Dorian, Mixolydian and Phrygian chorales raise problems when one attempts to sort them
into the tonal system… it seems more appropriate to refer each example to a related major or minor key,
because separating the chorales by modes or finales may fragment the data into rather sparse groups, and
the statistical results (particularly on phrase endings) would probably be diversified and less
significant."* He records that the literature is undecided — *"Daniel (2000:19) demonstrates that the
literature is undecided on this issue, and finally finds that both interpretations can be grounded by
equally legitimate reasons"* — and that the reduction is not a claim about the music: *"modal chorales are
nevertheless not reduced/subsumed into a major-minor system. They are transposed to C, but their
idiosyncratic harmonic features will be reflected in the statistical results."* **The counterweight is the
reason:** his ground is statistical power, ours is measured agreement with the annotators. **A convergent
decision taken for a different reason is weaker support than it looks, and is recorded as such.**

**Finding (6) — A RIVAL SHAPE FOR DP-E's SECOND HALF (*where may the tonality change*), AND A REPORTED
CASE THAT RUNS AGAINST OUR OWN D-337.** DP-E is **CHOSEN: with the chords; a tonality change is located at
a harmonic boundary** (`FRAMEWORK.md:712-714`, read whole), and **D-337** — read this session at the
`DECISIONS.md` INDEX row and **not** at its home in `decisions/group_H.md` — records that *a lean toward
another degree is a tonicization by default; a key change needs a confirming cadence AND persistence,
expressed as a change-cost*. **Row 23 reports a case where neither holds:** §7.1, on *"Jesu, Leiden, Pein und
Tod"* (B194), *"already the transition Eb – Bb – Cm suffices to produce a likely interpretation of
c-minor… there is no leading tone/dominant involved. In this case, for instance the pc set C-D-Eb-G
appears to suggest c-minor so distinctively that it overrides the Eb-major context."* He draws the
consequence himself: *"The classical notion of modulation, e.g. following Schönberg (1969; 1978),
necessarily includes the presence of a dominant or leading note context, which will have a stabilising
role. But here, a case of music practice is found where change of key is initiated and stabilised by
other means without central participation by a dominant."* **What bounds it, and it bounds it hard:** this
is one worked example, with no ground-truth analysis of that passage, produced by a model that reports no
accuracy figure at all. **It is a candidate question for DP-E and for D-337's persistence clause, not
evidence against either.**

**Finding (7) — THE UNCERTAINTY PRACTICE, RECORDED AS THE INVENTORY TRACKS IT.** The paper reports
standard deviations beside every mean in Table 5.8 and p-values with degrees of freedom on the
correlations it takes from Krumhansl. **It reports no uncertainty of any kind on its own key induction,
because it reports no figure for it.** And it introduces two hand-set thresholds — the once-only *n*-gram
cut and the 90 % ambiguity margin — **neither fitted and neither ablated**, which is the shape of a
hand-declared constant silently doing a measurement's work. *(`DEFECT_TYPES.md` was NOT opened by this
side, so no catalog entry is named for that shape and none is claimed.)*

**Finding (8) — THE #20 POSITION, STATED EXACTLY.** No value that the paper's key induction
or its sliding-window model uses is fitted, and there is no held-out set anywhere in this paper, so #20
does not bind on those. *(★ CORRECTED 2026-09-20 on the user's ruling of that date, recorded in the
banner. FORMER WORDING, PRESERVED (#12): "There is no fit and no held-out set anywhere in this paper, so
#20 does not bind on it." **The paper does make one fit:** Diagram 5.11's caption (PDF page 100) reads
"Zipf plots and least square fits with Simon's (1955) formula for n-grams with n = 1,2,3,4,5,6", and
§3(e) above lists those fits among the analyses. The second reader met no fitted parameter and no
goodness-of-fit value for them in the pages as read, and nothing in the paper is graded on them. Ground:

**Finding (9) — THE GROUND TRUTH, NAMED: THERE IS NONE.** Recorded here as its own finding rather than

## 2. The input and the repertoire, established at page 1 and at the paper's own data section (e⁸)

**The input is CHORD SYMBOLS** — established at page 1 by (c⁸) and again here at §3 and §5.1. §3
defines a sequence as *"x = x_{1:N} = (x_1, …, x_N), where each x_n takes values in the set of chord
symbols (output symbol space) Ω"*; §1 says in terms *"we use chord-sequence data in the popular/jazz
notation"* and that *"the method is independent of particular music styles or systems of chord
notation and is applicable to other chord notations such as the Roman numeral notation and the
figured bass notation."* **No notes, no score and no audio enter any model the paper runs**; §5.5's Figure 13 sketches,
without running it, a chord model joined to a feature model for recognition.

**Two datasets, §5.1 (page 8), and PCFG models were run on only one of them:**

- **J-pop:** chord sequences of **3500 J-pop songs** from a public web page (footnote 3: J-Total
  Music). *"All songs had key information in the major mode and were transposed to C major key. Each
  sequence in this dataset corresponds to a whole piece and the average length was 119.5 (chords)."*
  **"The computation time required for learning and inferring PCFG models using such long sequences
  is practically too large and only Markov models and HMMs were tested using this data."**
- **Billboard:** sequences extracted from the McGill **Billboard dataset** (reference [48], Burgoyne,
  Wild & Fujinaga 2011), sampled from the Billboard Hot 100 of 1958–1991. *"Using the musical
  structure annotation, 1702 chord sequences with a length larger than 7 were obtained by segmenting
  468 popular pieces in units of sections such as verse and chorus."* Tonic transposed to C; because
  the Billboard data has tonic but not mode, *"the obtained sequences included C minor sequences as
  well as more frequent C major sequences."* Average length **13.0**. **"We tested all types of models
  using this dataset."**
- **Splits:** test data 500 J-pop sequences and 171 Billboard sequences (one tenth); training
  subsets of 30, 300 and 3000 (J-pop) and 30, 300 and 1531 (Billboard) sequences.
- **Symbol spaces:** the top 10, 20 or 50 chord symbols per dataset with every other symbol mapped to
  *Other*, giving N_Ω = 10+1, 20+1, 50+1. Tables 2 and 3 (pages 8–9) list the symbols and the
  cumulative proportions: J-pop 79.75 % / 90.92 % / 98.20 %, Billboard 58.42 % / 69.55 % / 84.89 %.

**So the repertoire is popular music — Japanese pop and Anglo-American chart pop — as chord symbols,
with the tonality removed as a variable by transposition to C.** That last clause matters for L2:
the paper's models answer *what chord follows what* inside a fixed tonic, and the tonality question
the L2 charter entangles with it (`FRAMEWORK.md` L2, *"what is the tonality at each moment"*) is not
present in their input at all.

**The paper holds NO harmonic ground truth.** No Roman numeral, no functional label and no analyst's
reading is annotated on either dataset. The words *tonic*, *dominant* and *subdominant* appear in §5.4.2
as the authors' own interpretation of learned categories — Figure 11's caption says *"States are
manually sorted for clearer illustration"* — and nowhere as a target the models are graded against.
The *"ground-truth symbol"* of §4.2 (equation 31) is the **next chord symbol in the data**, not an
analysis label.

## 4. The record's three joined claims, each answered separately at the object (e⁸)

The record's *against* sentence, quoted whole from `FRAMEWORK.md` **line 794–797** (DP-O, read at
the object this sitting): *"Against it: tree models are harder to optimise and *often perform no
better* than latent-category sequence models of matched size, and induced categories correspond to
textbook harmonic functions only while the models are small. [FACT — both.]"* And from **line
1865–1868** (§S6's DP15, read at the object this sitting): *"Against it, Tsushima and colleagues find
that their tree models are harder to optimise and *often perform no better* than latent-category
sequence models of matched size, and that induced categories correspond to textbook harmonic
functions only while the models are small. [FACT.]"*

**Claim 1 — "tree models are harder to optimise." SUPPORTED; part MEASURED, part ASSERTED, and the
paper's own word is *difficulty* rather than *harder*.**
- *Measured:* §5.3 (page 15), on the Billboard data at N_Ω = 20+1, Figures 8 and 9: *"For N_X = 300
  and 1531, the PCFG models worked at most equivalently and often worse than the HMMs with N_Γ = N_Δ.
  There is a clear tendency that the HMM initialisations yielded better results than the random
  initialisations in the range 4 ≤ N_Δ ≤ 10. These results show the difficulty of parameter
  optimisation for PCFG models and the effectiveness of the HMM initialisation in some cases."* And,
  closing §5.3 (page 16): *"These results again confirm that there are many local optima for the
  PCFG-model parameters and it is difficult to find good optima by random initialisation even with the
  GS algorithm."* Figure 9 shows the spread of test-data perplexity across initialisations per
  PCFG size.
- *Asserted:* §4.1 (page 6), citing reference [39]: *"It has been reported that the initialisation
  problem is more severe for PCFG models than HMMs because of the complex model structure and the
  existence of many local optima."* And §5.5 (page 18): *"the PCFG models require time complexity of
  square order with respect to the sequence length and cubic order with respect to the number of
  nonterminals, which is typically much larger than that of HMMs"* — a complexity statement, not a
  timing measurement — with §5.1's consequence that the PCFG models **could not be run on the J-pop
  data at all** for cost.
- *Bound:* the measured half is on one dataset (Billboard), at one symbol space shown (N_Ω = 20+1,
  §5.3 saying *"the results for other cases were similar"*), with **30 random seeds for N_Δ ≤ 6 and 4
  to 6 seeds for N_Δ ≥ 7** because of computation time.

**Claim 2 — "often perform no better than latent-category sequence models of matched size."
SUPPORTED at the object and MEASURED — but *matched size* means matched STATE COUNT, which is not
matched capacity, and the axis is predictive power.**
- *Measured:* §5.3 (page 15): *"For N_X = 300 and 1531, the PCFG models worked at most equivalently
  and often worse than the HMMs with N_Γ = N_Δ"* (test-data perplexity); *"For error rates, we again
  find that overall the PCFG models worked at most equivalently and often worse than the HMMs with
  N_Γ = N_Δ."* §5.5 (page 18): *"Given the result that PCFG models did not much improve the
  predictive power of chord sequences compared to HMMs, there would be little interest in using PCFG
  models for simple recognition tasks."* Two qualifications the paper states beside it: *"for N_X = 30
  and 300, the lowest test-data perplexity for the PCFG models was less than that of the Markov
  models"*, and *"The lowest error rate for the PCFG models was less than that of the Markov models
  for N_X = 30 and they were even for N_X = 300."*
- *What "matched size" is at the object:* the comparison sets **N_Γ = N_Δ** — the same number of
  latent states as nonterminals (Figure 8's horizontal axis is *"Model size N_Γ/N_Δ"*). **It is not
  matched parameter count.** Table 1 (page 4) gives the free-parameter counts: HMM
  (1+N_Γ)(N_Γ−1)+N_Γ(N_Ω−1); PCFG (1+N_Δ)(N_Δ²−1)+N_Δ N_Ω. At equal N the PCFG carries more
  parameters, the difference growing with N. **So the record's phrase *matched size* is the paper's
  own matching and is right as far as it goes; the record's falsifier two lines below says
  *matched-capacity*, and the paper's comparison is not that.** See §7, finding (3).
- *The axis:* **predictive power over the next chord symbol** — perplexity and symbol-wise error rate
  on held-out chord sequences. No harmonic ground truth is involved (§2 above). The falsifier's axis
  is *"this repertoire's ground truth"*. See §7, finding (5).
- *Bound:* Billboard data only; PCFG models were not run on J-pop.

**Claim 3 — "induced categories correspond to textbook harmonic functions only while the models are
small." PARTLY SUPPORTED, ASSERTED by inspection rather than measured — and the word *only* is the
record's, not the paper's.**
- *What the paper says:* Abstract: *"the self-emergent categories often correspond to traditional
  harmonic functions."* §1 (page 2): *"the learned categories often correspond to traditional
  harmonic functions when the model size is small, which confirms the results of unsupervised chord
  categorisation [42, 43]."* §6: *"the learned categories often corresponded to traditional harmonic
  functions when the model size is small."* §5.4.2 (page 17), on Figure 11 — an HMM with N_Γ = 4 on
  J-pop and a PCFG with N_Δ = 5 on Billboard: *"The first three states/nonterminals in these examples
  can be identified as the tonic, subdominant, and dominant functions"*; *"Depending on initial
  parameters, for both HMMs and PCFG models, the learned categories were not always related to
  traditional harmonic functions as clearly as the above examples."*
- *How it is established:* **by the authors' inspection of two hand-sorted examples** (Figure 11,
  *"States are manually sorted"*) and one transition diagram (Figure 12, the four-state HMM read as
  *"a probabilistic representation of the familiar cadence structure"*). **No quantitative measure of
  correspondence to harmonic functions is defined or reported anywhere in the paper.** The
  information-theoretical measures of §5.4.1 describe how states are used, not whether they match a
  function label.
- *What the paper does NOT say:* it does not report that large models' categories **fail** to
  correspond. What §5.4.1 reports of larger HMMs (Figure 10, N_Γ up to 100) is that *"the same chord
  symbols are represented by multiple latent states depending on their context, which has a similar
  effect as symbol refinement for natural language models"* — a different observation. The paper's
  own qualifier on non-correspondence is **initialisation**, not size: *"Depending on initial
  parameters … not always related … as clearly."*
- *Two wording differences:* the record writes **textbook**; the paper writes **traditional**
  throughout. The record writes **only while small**, an exclusive claim; the paper writes **often
  … when small**, a frequency claim with no statement about large models. **The exclusive form is
  not in the paper.** See §7, finding (2).

**The `[FACT — both]` tag, read against this.** Claims 1 and 2 are stated and measured in the paper
(with the size/capacity and axis bounds above). Claim 3 is stated in the paper in a weaker form
than the record carries. **So the tag is right that all three are the paper's statements; it does
not by itself distinguish a measured result from an inspected example, and for claim 3 the record's
sentence is wider than the paper's.**

## 5. What the paper reports, and what each figure is a figure OF

**The paper prints almost no numerical result in its text.** Its numerical results are Figures 2–10 —
curves of test-data perplexity, error rate and the information measures against parameter count or
model size, for two datasets, three symbol spaces and three training sizes, over Markov models under
three smoothings, HMMs under EM and GS, and PCFG models under random and HMM initialisation — and
Figures 11–12 show learned categories; **the result curves' vertical axes carry no numeric tick
labels in the held rendering**, so no perplexity or error-rate
value can be transcribed from them. What is printed as a number:

- Tables 2 and 3: the most frequent chord symbols per dataset and the cumulative proportions quoted
  at §2 above.
- The dataset figures quoted at §2 (3500; 119.5; 1702; 468; 13.0; 500; 171; 30/300/3000; 30/300/1531).
- Learning constants: additive smoothing 0.1; Dirichlet parameter 0.1; η = 0.01/N_Δ; κ = 0.5416
  from equation 28 on the data; at most 500 (HMM) or 200 (PCFG) EM iterations, 500 (200) GS
  samplings, 50 polishing EM iterations, convergence at relative likelihood difference 10⁻⁵; 30
  random seeds for N_Γ ≤ 20 and 10 otherwise; PCFG seeds as at §4.
- Qualitative results in words: *"for all N_X and for all N_Ω, the lowest test-data perplexity by the
  HMMs was less than the lowest value by the Markov models"* on the J-pop data; overfitting for N_X = 30 and 300 at
  some N_Γ between 1 and 100; for N_X = 3000 both quantities still decreasing at N_Γ = 100; on Billboard at
  N_X = 1531 and N_Ω = 20+1 and 50+1 the third-order Markov models *"less than or similar to the best
  results for the HMMs"*; *"If the perplexities or error rates for models with similar numbers of
  parameters are compared, HMMs consistently outperformed Markov models"*; GS better than EM for
  N_X = 1531 and N_Δ ≥ 50 (this last figure is as printed on page 9, though N_Δ elsewhere reaches
  20 — recorded as printed, not reconciled); §5.2.2's conclusion that *"training data of size N_X ≥
  300 were able to accurately predict the optimal model for unseen data for model sizes without
  overfitting"*; §5.3's PCFG-against-HMM
  result at §4 above; §5.4.1's P_Γ rising *"roughly proportionally to the model size"*, P_φ falling
  with size but *"larger than 2 even for N_Γ = 100"*, V rising, P_π rising slowly.

**Every figure is a figure of predictive power over chord-symbol sequences in pop repertoire, or of
a learned model's internal structure. None is an accuracy against a human harmonic analysis, none is
a tree accuracy, and none is on this project's repertoire.** The record cites this paper by
characterisation and by no figure (§6 below), which is consistent with the paper printing none of
the kind the record cites.

## 7. The findings, each with what it is a candidate for and what bounds it

**Finding (1) — THE LIVE DP-O CARRIES ROW 25's CHARACTERISATION WITHOUT NAMING ITS SOURCE; THE SEALED
DP15 NAMES IT.** Read at the object: `FRAMEWORK.md` 794–797 attributes the *against* sentence to no
work; 1865–1868 attributes it to *Tsushima and colleagues*. **Row 51's extract recorded this (its
lines 68–72) and this sitting confirms it at `FRAMEWORK.md`'s own lines.** *What it is a candidate
for:* a citation finding routed to the bibliography reconciliation, which the commission's §4 names
as its own act — *"New citation findings join the routed list."* *What bounds it:* DP-O's *for* half
is unattributed in the same way (row 21's paper is named at DP15, line 1862, and not at DP-O), so
this is the live section's convention and not a defect peculiar to row 25. **Nothing is changed:
§4 reserves every correction to `FRAMEWORK.md` to the user.**

**Finding (2) — THE RECORD'S THIRD CLAIM IS WIDER THAN THE PAPER'S, IN ONE WORD.** The paper says the
learned categories *often* correspond to *traditional* harmonic functions *when the model size is
small*, and that non-correspondence depends on *initial parameters*; it reports no failure of
correspondence at large size and measures correspondence by no quantity (§4, claim 3). The record's
sentence says they correspond *only while* the models are small. **The exclusive *only* is not in
the paper; *textbook* is not the paper's word.** *What it is a candidate for:* a wording correction
to the two `[FACT]` sentences, which under the commission's §4 is the user's to make on a surface.
*What bounds it:* the paper's own §5.4.1 does report that larger HMMs use *"multiple latent states
… depending on their context"* to represent the same symbol, which a reader could gloss as
categories drifting from functions as size grows — **but the paper does not draw that conclusion,
and this extract does not draw it for it.** Whether a characterisation at an underived point is a
commissioned verification target is the (b⁸) question, still the user's (§9).

**Finding (3) — NEITHER HALF OF DP-O'S EVIDENCE IS ON THE AXIS DP-O'S OWN FALSIFIER SETS.** The
falsifier (lines 798–800, 1870–1872): *"a tree model beating a matched-capacity sequence model on
this repertoire's ground truth, measured on the same corpus and the same axis."* **The *against* half
(row 25) matches by state count, not by capacity** — N_Γ = N_Δ with the PCFG carrying more parameters
at every N (Table 1) — **and its axis is predictive power over chord symbols, not a ground truth.**
**The *for* half (row 21), on that row's extract at its lines 463–475 and 506–512, compares a PCFG
against other grammars and degenerate trees with no sequence model in the comparison, at a 12-fold
parameter mismatch in the winner's disfavour, on Jazz lead sheets against 13 author-annotated
pieces.** *What it is a candidate for:* the user's question at (e⁸) — see finding (5). *What bounds
it:* this is a reading of two extracts and one framework span; row 21's half is taken from row 21's
extract and not from row 21's paper, which this side did not open.

**Finding (4) — CLAIMS 1 AND 2 HOLD AT THE OBJECT, WITH THEIR BOUNDS.** *Harder to optimise*: measured
as initialisation sensitivity and local optima on Billboard (Figures 8–9, §5.3) and asserted as
complexity order (§5.5), with the practical consequence that the tree models could not be run on the
longer dataset at all. *Often perform no better*: measured on Billboard at N_Ω = 20+1 in both
perplexity and error rate, with the paper's own two qualifications (better than the Markov models at
small training sizes). **No correction to the record's first two claims is found beyond the
size/capacity distinction at finding (3).**

**Finding (5) — WHETHER DP-O'S TWO HALVES CAN BE COMPARED AT ALL: THE FACTS, PUT TO THE USER.** (e⁸)
asks this and says it is a question about the record, not about either paper, and is his. The
facts, one column each:
- **Corpus.** Row 21: Jazz standards from the iRealPro collection as lead-sheet chord symbols (row
  21's extract, line 511). Row 25: J-pop chord sequences from a web page and Billboard chart-pop
  sections, transposed to C (this extract §2).
- **Metric.** Row 21: tree-span precision over internal nodes against 13 pieces annotated by the
  authors (row 21's extract, line 512). Row 25: test-data perplexity, symbol-wise predictive error
  rate and RMRR on held-out chord sequences (§3, §4.2 of the paper).
- **Axis.** Row 21: agreement of a parse tree with a human tree annotation. Row 25: prediction of the
  next chord symbol from its neighbours. **Neither is *this repertoire's ground truth*, and they are
  not the same axis as each other.**
- **Comparands.** Row 21: grammar against grammar and against degenerate trees. Row 25: grammar
  against latent-category sequence model, and both against Markov models.
**So the two halves of DP-O's sentence rest on two corpora, two metrics, two axes and two different
kinds of comparison.** Whether that makes the *for* and *against* halves incommensurable, or merely
two separate facts about two systems, is what he is asked to rule; this extract states it and
decides nothing. **DP-O's verdict — NONE CHOSEN, open — is untouched by either reading**, and the
commission's §5 STOP, quoted whole at §9, does not fire.

**Finding (6) — AN ADDITION CANDIDATE TO D-533's GROUND, WHICH CITES A CLASS AND NAMES NO WORK.** D-533
(read whole at `decisions/group_A.md` 703–729, **LIVE**, decided 2026-07-19, ratified by user) scores a
rare continuation by dividing the row's leftover in proportion to each chord's overall frequency,
and its *Why* is *"the standard construction in published back-off models of sequences (#1)"* — a
class with no work named, as row 23's extract already found at its finding (1). Row 25 §3.1 names the
construction's literature on chord sequences: additive smoothing, and Kneser–Ney and modified
Kneser–Ney, *"which incrementally use lower-order transition probabilities to obtain higher-order
transition probabilities"*, grounded in Chen & Goodman 1999 [31]. *What bounds it:* KN and MKN are
discounting-and-interpolation constructions over Markov orders and are not the same arithmetic as
D-533's proportional division of a leftover; the repertoire is pop chord symbols; and row 25 reports
no result that separates the three smoothings in its text. **It is a candidate citation to the CLASS
D-533's ground names, not to its mechanism, and it does not discharge the missing citation.**

**Finding (7) — THE LATENT-CATEGORY SHAPE, FOR THE L2 DETAIL SPECIFICATION'S CHORD-TRANSITION
QUESTION.** The row's admission reason is *"a method that learns the chord-sequence structure rather
than being given it."* What the paper supplies: a chord-transition model with a **learned** category
layer between chord symbols and their sequence structure (§3.2), evidence on two pop datasets that
such a layer predicts chord sequences better than a Markov model of comparable parameter count
(§5.2), and §5.5's Figure 13 — a *chord HMM + feature model*, where the latent categories sit above
chord symbols and the symbols emit features — as the shape for using it inside a recognition
system. *What bounds it, and the bounds are structural:* the categories are learned **inside a fixed
tonic** (§2), so the model does not carry the tonality the L2 charter entangles with chord
succession; the symbols are pop chord symbols, not degrees against a tonality; and D-532/D-533's
transition table is **counted from ground-truth annotations** with a ratified pooling ladder, which
is a supervised construction the paper's unsupervised one does not resemble. **It is a candidate
for the L2 detail specification to argue against or draw on, not a candidate architecture for this
project's repertoire.**

**Finding (8) — THE REFERENCE LIST REACHES HELD AND UNHELD ROWS.** Of the paper's 49 references, read
at pages 20–22: **[20] Raphael & Stoddard 2004**, *"Functional Harmonic Analysis Using Probabilistic
Models"*, CMJ 28(3), is candidacy row 2 (bibliography line 16, paywalled, not held); **[21] Temperley
2009**, JNMR 38(1), is candidacy row 8 (read, extracted); *(★ these two were ADDED at a re-landing after
the progress record's not-fetched paragraph for this row was written against the same pages and found
them — the first landing of this finding named neither, an omission recorded at §11)*; **[23]
Rohrmeier 2011** is candidacy row 22 (bibliography line 36, held, unread);
**[42] Rohrmeier & Cross 2008** is row 24 (NOT ADMITTED, not held); **[48] Burgoyne, Wild & Fujinaga
2011** is the Billboard dataset paper and is **not** the bibliography's Burgoyne, Pugin, Kereliuk &

*"An Information Theoretic Approach to Chord Categorization and Functional Harmony"*, is one of the two
papers (with [42]) the authors cite for the prior result that *"chord categories similar to
traditional harmonic functions were automatically obtained"* by unsupervised learning, and **is in neither the bibliography nor the candidacy table** (swept
on *Jacoby* and *Tymoczko*); likewise **[24] Granroth & Steedman 2012** and **[19] Steedman 1984**
(swept on *Granroth* and *Steedman*). *What it is a candidate for:* the bibliography reconciliation's

## 2. The input and the repertoire, established at page 1 and at the paper's own examples

**There is no data section.** The paper is a theoretical proposal (its own word at §6, printed page 47:
*"this paper mainly aims to make a programmatic theoretical contribution by proposing a generative
syntax account of tonal harmonic progressions"*), and its inputs are the inputs of its worked examples.

- **What the grammar operates on**: **chord symbols** and **scale degrees under a key** — the surface
  symbols 𝕆 = {*Cmaj, Cmin, C⁰, C^ø, …*} (page 39, §3), the scale degrees 𝕊 = {*I, II, …, VII, V/I, VII/I,
  …*} and the key symbols 𝕂 = {*Cmaj, Cmin, C♯maj, …*}. **Not notes, not a spelled score, not audio.**
- **What it does NOT operate on, in its own words** (page 45): *"the chord symbols in the analysis do
  not incorporate figured bass notation or chord inversions since such differences as well as resulting
  features of the underlying bass movement need to be modelled independently"*; and (page 43), after
  naming voice-leading rules and altered-chord derivations, *"The description of the specific details
  of specialized and stylistic rules will be a matter of fine-grained style-specific rules that do not
  belong to the general formalism presented here"*. *(★ CORRECTED 2026-09-20 at the cross-check. FORMER
  WORDING, PRESERVED (#12): the voice-leading rules and altered-chord derivations *"are a matter of
  fine-grained style-specific rules that do not belong to the general formalism presented here"* — the
  quotation's first two words were not the page's, and the page's subject is the description of
  specialized and stylistic rules.)* **So the grammar is inversion-blind,
  bass-blind and voicing-blind by declared scope.**
- **The worked examples, each a hand analysis and none a measurement**: Kostka & Payne's analysis of
  Haydn's Sonata No. 33, II (Figure 1, page 36 — relayed from Kostka & Payne, with the author's own
  footnote 1 disagreeing with it); the sequence *C A⁷ Dm G C* and nine variants, (b) to (j) (page 37, §2) *(★ the first writing said
  "ten variants", counting the base sequence (a) among them; corrected at the user-ordered second check)*; a phrase
  of the Bach chorale *Ermuntre Dich, mein schwacher Geist*, mm. 1–4 (Figure 3, page 44); the first
  phrase of the jazz standard *Autumn leaves* in two analyses (Figure 4, page 45); a phrase of
  Bortnianski's *Tebe Poëm* (Figure 5, page 46) *(★ CORRECTED 2026-09-20 at the cross-check: this file
  wrote "Bortniansky's" here and "the Bortniansky and Waldstein examples" in §3; Figure 5's caption
  prints "Bortnianski's")*; the opening of Beethoven's Waldstein sonata, op. 53, I,
  mm. 1–13 in reduction, two analyses (Figure 6, page 47).
- **Repertoire, as stated**: the grammar is offered for *"diatonic harmonic progressions"* (abstract)
  and *"a core set of rules describing core tonal phrases and the relationship between keys and
  modulations"* (page 36); the phrase-level rules 1 and 2 are *"designed in order to match
  phrase-based forms of harmony, as in Jazz or in pop music"* (page 39), and rule 3 is offered as the
  alternative for common-practice pieces treated as a single tonic prolongation. **The examples span
  common-practice (Haydn, Bach, Beethoven), a Russian sacred piece and a jazz standard; the paper claims
  no repertoire bound and measures on none.**
- **Ground truth: NONE.** No corpus, no annotation, no agreement figure, no accuracy of any kind.

**Domain bound owed?** The input is symbolic (chord symbols and scale degrees), so no audio-domain
bound is owed. **What IS owed and stated: the grammar's input is one level above this project's L2
input.** L2 reads notes and decides segmentation, tonality, degree, chord and (per the record) inversion
and bass; this grammar takes chord symbols already segmented and already keyed (every symbol carries a
key property, rule 15's paragraph, page 41) and decides their dependency structure. **The tonality L2
entangles with chord succession is an INPUT here, not an output**, as it was for row 25 by a different
route (there, transposed away; here, given).

## 4. What the record's *for* sentence takes from this paper, and what it does not — answered at the object

**The record's sentence, quoted whole from `FRAMEWORK.md` at both homes, read at the file this
sitting.** DP-O, lines 790–800: *"**NONE CHOSEN — underived: open, and deliberately not foreclosed.**
For it: a recursive grammar represents something a flat sequence cannot — the same surface chords
functioning simultaneously as a tonic phrase in one tonality and a dominant phrase in another — with
tree accuracy 45.95% against 39.43% for a non-transposition-tied grammar and under 10% for a
right-branching baseline. Against it: tree models are harder to optimise and *often perform no better*
than latent-category sequence models of matched size, and induced categories correspond to textbook
harmonic functions only while the models are small. [FACT — both.] **The decomposition neither adopts
a hierarchy nor forecloses one**: what chord follows what is inside L2's charter, and a grammar is one
way to answer it. *The falsifier:* a tree model beating a matched-capacity sequence model on this
repertoire's ground truth, measured on the same corpus and the same axis."* DP15, lines 1861–1872,
carries the same two halves with the *for* half attributed to *"Harasim and colleagues"* and each half
marked *"[FACT.]"* separately. **`FRAMEWORK.md` names Rohrmeier nowhere — a grep of the file on
*Rohrmeier* returns no line.**

**The three parts of the *for* half, each answered at this paper:**

1. **The representational claim — *"a recursive grammar represents something a flat sequence cannot —
   the same surface chords functioning simultaneously as a tonic phrase in one tonality and a dominant
   phrase in another."*** **STATED IN THIS PAPER, in its own words and as its own preferred analysis:**
   the modulation rule's paragraph (page 41) — *"the double generation of the pivot chord from two
   different branches of the parse tree constitutes the preferred form of analysis that captures the
   double role of the pivot chord"* — and the Bach chorale analysis (page 45, Figure 3): *"the chord is
   derived twice from the respective adjacent branches of the different parent derivations"*, the '='
   signs in the figure marking *"both instances of the G chord [that] refer to the identical surface
   pivot chord"*. The pages 49–50 argument gives the contrast with the flat sequence in the author's
   words (the Markov model's *"Brownian" harmonic motion*, the exponential data a prolongation would
   need). **Row 21's extract established (its lines 451–455, read this sitting) that the same
   illustration is in row 21's paper's own words too, on *Afternoon in Paris*.** So the claim is in
   both papers; **this one is the earlier, and the one row 21's grammar says it follows** (row 21's
   extract line 778, a relay of row 21's §4 — this side did not open row 21's paper).
2. **The three figures — 45.95%, 39.43%, under 10%.** **NOT IN THIS PAPER.** The paper prints no
   accuracy, no percentage, no corpus size, no count and no test statistic anywhere in its 20 pages
   (§5 below). They are row 21's, verified there at its §6.2 (row 21's extract, its figure-by-figure
   table at lines 424–434, a relay).
3. **The `[FACT]` marker.** At DP-O one marker covers both halves; at DP15 the *for* half's marker
   stands after the figures. **What this paper can support is a THEORY marker on part 1, under the
   theory-grounding corollary's own vocabulary (`CLAUDE.md` Guiding principles: *"THEORY (established
   published theory)"*), not a FACT marker on a measurement** — this paper measures nothing. Whether
   the record's *"[FACT — both.]"* is meant of the figures alone or of the whole sentence is not
   settled by the sentence, and row 21's finding (1) already puts the joining of the representational
   claim to the figures to the user as a corrected-structural-claim candidate. **This read adds a
   citation fact to that open question and decides nothing about it.**

**The falsifier — *a tree model beating a matched-capacity sequence model on this repertoire's ground
truth, measured on the same corpus and the same axis*.** **This paper supplies nothing toward it and
claims nothing toward it**: no model is trained, no capacity is stated, no corpus is used, no ground
truth exists, and the paper's own §6 says the cognitive reality of recursive dependencies on the
largest levels *"cannot be taken for granted"* (page 50) and that some of the rules proposed *"may be
arguable"* (page 47). *(★ CORRECTED 2026-09-20 UNDER THE USER'S RULING. FORMER WORDING, PRESERVED (#12):
"says the grammar's cognitive reality *"cannot be taken for granted"* and that its rules *"may be
arguable"*" — the page limits the first to "the largest levels" and the second to "some of the rules
proposed".)* **What it supplies is the theoretical case the
falsifier would test** — the pages 49–50 argument that Markov and n-gram models cannot express
prolongation and return-to-key — in the form of an argument, not a measurement.

## 2. The input, the output and the repertoire, established at page 1 and at the paper's own data section

- **What the models operate on**: **chord symbols** from **jazz lead sheets** — page 1: *"a formal
  grammar of jazz chord sequences"*; page 3, §2.2: *"jazz standards are rarely transcribed as full
  scores, but are more analytically notated as a melody with accompanying chord sequence. Analysing the
  harmonic structures underlying chord sequences, rather than streams of notes, avoids some difficult
  practical issues such as voice leading and performance styles"*. **Not notes, not a score, not audio.**
- **What the models DECIDE**: for each chord symbol, a **position in the two-dimensional tonal space**
  (a path through the space traced by the chord roots, §3.3, page 4) and a **cadential function** — the
  chord's role as dominant, subdominant or tonic in a tension–resolution structure (§2.1, page 2; the
  evaluation credits *"the function"* per point, §6.1, page 7). **The paper decides NO tonality label, NO
  segmentation, NO chord identity, NO inversion and NO bass.** Page 8 says so in the paper's own words:
  *"A certain amount of analysis has already gone into the process of producing these chord symbols: a
  human has divided the music into time segments of constant harmony, selected the most prominent notes,
  and narrowed down the range of possible chord roots somewhat."* **Tonality is neither an input nor an
  output here** — the tonal-space path stands in for it, and the pitch information the fitted models
  use is RELATIVE: the supertagger's emissions are *"a pair of the chord type and the interval between
  this chord's and the previous chord's roots"* so that *"the model account[s] only for relative pitch"*
  (§5.2, page 6), and the baseline's states are deviations from a path built root by root (§5.4, page 6).
  So the tonality L2 entangles with chord succession is absent by construction, as it was for row 25 by
  transposition and for row 22 by being given.
- **Repertoire, as stated**: **tonal jazz standards** — §2.2 gives three reasons for the genre: large
  extended cadences with complex embedding; contrafacts; lead-sheet notation. The lexicon is *"specific
  to the genre"* and *"A lexicon for European baroque music, for example, would not use all of the
  substitution categories included in the jazz lexicon and would require some additional categories to
  reflect different conventional expressions of the perfect cadence"* (page 5). **The paper claims its
  approach is not limited to the domain (page 3) and measures on no other.**
- **Corpus (§5.1, page 5)**: **76 chord sequences, roughly 3,000 chords**, chosen from lead sheets,
  **"excluding certain sequences that could not be analysed using our grammar, due to limitations of the
  lexicon (e.g. rare substitutions not covered)"**; hand-annotated with one lexical category per chord
  and with the points of coordination, *"providing sufficient information to define a unique tonal space
  analysis of every sequence"*; **no held-out test set** — 10-fold cross-validation (§6.2, page 7); the
  authors *"plan to make the corpus publicly available in the future"*. **Whether it was released is not
  known to this read; no web access was made.**
- **Ground truth**: the paper's gold standard is its own hand annotation of tonal-space paths and
  functions over those 76 sequences. **It is a ground truth of the paper's own axis, on jazz lead
  sheets; it is not this repertoire's ground truth and it carries no Roman numeral, no key label and no
  chord label of the record's kind.**

**Domain bound owed?** The input is symbolic (chord symbols), so no audio-domain bound is owed. **What IS
owed and stated: the input is one level above L2's** — chord symbols already segmented by a human, as
for rows 21, 22 and 25 — and the OUTPUT is on an axis L2 does not publish (tonal-space position) plus one
it does not publish directly either (cadential function; the record's function layer is L5's, D-335).

bass and no chord-tone assignment; its input is jazz lead-sheet chord symbols already segmented by a
human; its output is on an axis the record does not publish (a tonal-space path) plus a cadential
