nowhere in the staged tree; `FRAMEWORK.md` names it nowhere by the terms run, by no characterisation
and by no figure; and its
lexicon is hand-crafted and, by the authors' own statement, genre-specific. Its bearing on the record is
as a third measured system at an underived, open design point — meeting the falsifier on two clauses of
five — plus four candidates for grounds and defenses (findings 3, 4, 5, 7) and a record precision
(finding 9). **That is the shape row 25's extract graded NOT CENTRAL (its §10, read this sitting):
evidence at DP-O, peripheral to this project's design.**

to rows 21, 22, 23 and 25 at their extracts and this paper — that reports a tree model AHEAD of a
sequence model on one corpus against a hand-annotated gold standard, which is the SHAPE of DP-O's

## 2. The input, the output and the repertoire — what the paper actually works on

**The paper is not an analysis system.** It takes as input a corpus **already annotated with a
vocabulary of "surface tokens"** and evaluates ways of grouping those tokens into a smaller set of
categories. Its own words (printed page 1, §1.1): *"Given a large corpus of music fully annotated with a
particular system of chord representation (surface tokens), our approach evaluates their possible
groupings or clusters into a more coarse-grained set of categories. Surface tokens can consist of Roman
numerals (Temperley, 2009; Tymoczko, 2003), scale degrees (De Clercq & Temperley, 2011; Huron, 2006) or
simultaneous MIDI sonorities (Quinn & Mavromatis, 2011; Rohrmeier, 2005). We take these pre-existing
representations as our starting point, without attempting to privilege any particular vocabulary."*

**What it decides and does not decide.** It decides **which grouping of an already-labelled chord
vocabulary is best on an accuracy-against-complexity trade-off**, and it derives the best groupings
("self-emergent" or "optimal" categories) from the corpus's own bigram statistics. **It decides no
tonality, no segmentation, no chord identity, no inversion, no bass and no chord-tone assignment.** Where
its input is MIDI (§2.3, printed pages 11–12), the segmentation into *"vertical sonorities or 'slices'"*,
the key-finding (*"the key-finding methodology of White and Quinn (2014), who used a Krumhansl–Schmuckler
key-finding algorithm on windows of eight slices"*) and the transposition to C are **done before its
method runs and by other authors' methods**; it then keeps *"the 22 most common sonorities (those that
comprise more than 1% of the dataset)"*.

**The corpora, as the paper names them (§2.4 and Appendix B, printed pages 12–13 and 23–26).** Sixteen
datasets: **eleven drawn from five published works** — *de Clercq & Temperley 2011; Huron 2006; Rohrmeier
& Cross 2008; Temperley 2009; Tymoczko 2011* — and **five new datasets constructed by author Tymoczko**.
Named at Tables B1–B4:

| Dataset | Source, as printed | Tokens |
|---|---|---|
| 1, 2 | Tymoczko (2011a), figure 7.1.6 page 230: major-mode / minor-mode Bach chorales | 7 scale degrees each |
| 3, 4 | Tymoczko (2011a), figure 7.1.6 page 230: 19 major-mode / 19 minor-mode Mozart piano sonatas | 7 each |
| 5 | Huron (2006), table 13.2 page 251: major-mode Baroque music | 7 |
| 6 | Temperley (2009) aggregate statistics (6/4 reanalysed): major-mode excerpts from Kostka & Payne's textbook *Tonal Harmony* | 12 |
| 7 | de Clercq & Temperley (2011), tables 2–3 pages 60–61: 100 major-mode Rock songs | 12 |
| 8 | the same data reduced to seven diatonic tokens; the row prints *"100 major/minor mode Rock songs"* | 7 |
| 9 | sequences of two adjacent chords from the same dataset; *"101 surface tokens"*, only common bigrams displayed | 101 |
| 10, 11 | Rohrmeier & Cross (2008), tables 1–2 pages 8–9: simultaneous transposed pitch classes from MIDI renditions of major-mode / minor-mode Bach chorales | 15 each |
| 12 | major-mode Bach chorales — *"52 surface tokens, 9527 total chords in the corpus"* | 52 |
| 13 | minor-mode Bach chorales — *"69 surface tokens, 5700 total chords"* | 69 |
| 14 | major-mode Mozart piano sonatas — *"38 surface tokens, 7826 total chords"* | 38 |
| 15 | minor-mode Mozart piano sonatas — *"40 surface tokens, 1602 total chords"* | 40 |
| 16 | Palestrina — Ionian, Mixolydian and Lydian passages in seven masses (printed page 13) | not printed at the table |

Beside these, the body names **dataset 1A** (printed pages 16 and 18): *"inversion-free two-chord
Roman-numeral progressions drawn from major-mode passages in all 371 chorales"*, *"drawn from all 371
chorales rather than the 70 in dataset 1, and also uses the accurate marginal distribution"*; and the
**MIDI dataset of §2.3** (printed pages 11–12, Table 4 and Figure 8): the Bach chorales from MIDI, reduced
to slices as above.

**Two printed inconsistencies inside the file about dataset 12, recorded and not resolved:** the body
(printed page 13) says dataset 12 *"consists of transition frequencies between the 49 major-mode diatonic
triads and sevenths (with bass notes)"* while Table B3 prints *"52 surface tokens"*; and the rock rows of
Table B2 print *"major-mode"* for dataset 7 and *"major/minor mode"* for datasets 8 and 9 of the same
songs. Recorded as printed; nothing here is used as a figure.

**Where the five new datasets came from, in the paper's own words — footnote 3, printed page 13:** *"The
first 70 chorales were compiled with the help of undergraduates in Tymoczko's MUS306 course at Princeton
University, as well as several graduate students (including Hamish Robb and Luis Valencia). For the
remaining 301 chorales, Tymoczko corrected analyses produced by Heinrich Taube's 'Chorale Composer'
software, as improved by Simon Krauss, an undergraduate thesis student of Tymoczko's. All data were then
thoroughly cross-validated using Michael Cuthbert's music21 toolkit, with all discrepancies further
analysed to locate possible errors."* The Mozart datasets were *"compiled with the assistance of more than
30 music theorists"* (printed page 13). The footnote continues past the sentences quoted with a

## 4. What the record's DP-O takes from this paper, and what it does not — answered at the object

**DP-O's *against* half (`FRAMEWORK.md` line 794–797, read this sitting):** *"tree models are harder to
optimise and often perform no better than latent-category sequence models of matched size, and induced
categories correspond to textbook harmonic functions only while the models are small. [FACT — both.]"*

the record names; this paper is what row 25's paper cites (its [43], with [42] Rohrmeier & Cross 2008)
for its sentence *"the learned categories often correspond to traditional harmonic functions when the
model size is small, which confirms the results of unsupervised chord categorisation [42, 43]"* (row 25's
extract, Claim 3, lines 263–266, read this sitting).** So the question is what THIS paper establishes
about categories corresponding to functions, and whether it supports the record's clause as worded.

**(a) That induced categories correspond to textbook harmonic functions — SUPPORTED at small category
counts, and by a measure this time.** The correspondence is stated in the paper's own words at §3 above
(dataset 1: the three-category optimum *"coincides with F_TSD"*; MIDI: *"clearly very similar"*; datasets
1–8: I, IV and V always in different clusters at three categories). **Unlike row 25's paper, whose
correspondence was established by the authors' inspection of hand-sorted examples (row 25's extract, line
272), this paper carries a quantitative measure of how far the textbook theory sits from the optimum: the

the plotted positions and the words *nearly optimal*, *very close*, *quite close*; and no spread, no
interval and no significance test attaches to any of it (§5).

Row 25's extract found that *only* is the record's word and not row 25's paper's (line 261–262). This
paper does not report that larger category counts FAIL to correspond; what it reports of its seven-category
optimum on dataset 12 is that it *"might seem to show that information-theoretic ideality diverges from
musical intuition"* at first glance and, *"on further reflection"*, carries *"the outline of familiar
functional ideas"* (T1/T2 tonic, S1/S2 subdominant, D1–D3 dominant); and it names *"grouping chords

size beyond which correspondence fails.** The record's *only* remains wider than either of its two

## 7. The findings, each with what it is a candidate for and what bounds it

**Finding (1) — What this paper establishes for the *against* half's third claim, and what it does
not.** *Candidate for:* the ground of DP-O's *against* half at `FRAMEWORK.md` line 794–797 and DP15's
attribution — as a precision, applied nowhere. *What it is:* this paper supports **correspondence of
data-derived categories to TSD at two to four categories**, on Bach, Mozart, Baroque, textbook and rock
corpora as annotated by others, with a quantitative measure (distance from the optimal curve) that row
25's paper lacked; it **does not assert, and does not measure, any size beyond which correspondence
fails — in the 26 pages as read, a reader's negative** — and reads its own seven-category optimum as functionally legible with deviations. **The record's
*only while the models are small* is therefore wider than both of its sources as this read and row 25's
read found them.** *Bound:* no spread, no interval, no test, no held-out split anywhere; the measure is
a plotted distance the paper does not print as a number; the corpora are not this repertoire's ground
truth as an object. *Applied nowhere:* DP-O's figures are the commission's §4 exclusion (quoted at §9);
this is a finding for the user.

**Finding (2) — A published, data-derived pooling of a chord vocabulary BY CONTINUATION BEHAVIOUR: an
addition candidate to the ground under D-532 and D-533.** *Candidate for:* the ground of **D-532** (the
chord-transition table's pooling level that groups a secondary dominant's continuations by their relation
to its target — LIVE, ratified by the user 2026-07-19, home `ARCHITECTURE.md`; read at `decisions/group_A.md`
lines 667–701 this sitting) and of **D-533** (rare continuations scored from the row's leftover in
proportion to overall frequency; lines 703–729). *What it is:* D-532 restores *"from counts"* a pooling
that groups chords by what they DO next; this paper is a published method whose whole output is groupings
of a chord vocabulary *"according to behaviour rather than sound"* (printed page 18), derived from the
same kind of object — a bigram table counted from an annotated corpus — by the information bottleneck,
with the number of categories chosen on an accuracy/complexity trade-off (§1.9–1.11). Its dataset-12
seven-category optimum (printed page 10) groups inversions and seventh forms of the same degree with
other degrees by their continuation, which is the shape of pooling a transition table's rare rows into
behaviourally alike classes. *Bound:* the paper's categories are a description of a corpus, not a
back-off scheme inside a decoder, and it says nothing about scoring an unseen continuation; its pooling
is over Roman-numeral tokens already keyed to a tonality, where D-532's is over a secondary dominant's
relation to its target across transpositions; no figure of this paper occurs in the record. **This is
precedent (#1) for deriving a pooling level from counts rather than by hand — not a proposal to adopt the
method, and not a claim that D-532's ratified pooling is wrong.** Recorded beside row 65's finding (4) —
the *Dom* schema and the supertagger's emissions as relational representation — and merged with neither.

**Finding (3) — Published support that the three-role summary is DERIVABLE from the Roman-numeral
stream: an addition candidate to the ground under D-335 and to the D-586 paragraph.** *Candidate for:*
**D-335** (*"The function layer outputs the Roman numeral; the tonic/subdominant/dominant summary is a
derived read-out, never a stored output"* — LIVE, ratified 2026-08-02, home
`cowork_layer5_function_design.md` §9, read at `DECISIONS.md` line 524 this sitting; the home file was
not opened) and **D-586**'s paragraph at `ARCHITECTURE.md` lines 2127–2137, whose last clause reads
*"where the three-role labels exist at all they are a deterministic lookup from the Roman numeral"*.
*What it is:* this paper is a published work in which the three roles are NOT a lookup but the optimal
three-way compression of the Roman-numeral stream's own bigram statistics, and in which that optimum
*"coincides with"* the textbook TSD on dataset 1 and places I, IV and V apart on datasets 1–8 — **so the
record's position that the summary is derived from the Roman numeral gains a published instance where
the derivation is statistical rather than by rule, and comes out at the textbook answer.** *Bound:*
D-586's survey clause is about autonomous Roman-numeral systems and this paper is not one (it takes Roman
numerals as input), so nothing here contradicts D-586; the coincidence is at three categories on
particular corpora; deviations are named by the paper (I with ii on datasets 3, 4, 6; IV alone in rock;
I⁴ as dominant on MIDI). *Applied nowhere.*

**Finding (4) — A THIRD sense of *function* beside D-586's two and row 22's and row 65's findings.**
*Candidate for:* the D-586 paragraph's ground, as a precision, applied nowhere. *What it is:* D-586 says
*function* in the machine-learning literature names the Roman-numeral components, not Riemann's
three-role theory. Row 22's finding (7) and row 65's finding (3) recorded the cadential-role sense.
**This paper uses *functional harmony* in the THREE-ROLE sense (tonic/subdominant/dominant — its Table 1,
Figure 2, and §§2.1–2.4 and 2.7 as read) AND defines a function operationally as a category that maximises the mutual
information between the current chord and its local context** — *"functional harmony can be analysed as a
clustering problem"* (abstract); *"to be a dominant chord is to a significant extent a matter of acting
like a dominant chord; that is, to move authentically to I and I⁶ and, less often, deceptively to IV⁶ and
vi"* (printed page 14). *Bound:* a definition the paper proposes for its own framework; a reader of the
survey behind D-586 meets it as one paper's usage and not as the literature's.

**Finding (5) — The paper's own account of the limits of its categories: behaviour, not sound; local
context only.** *Candidate for:* the ground under DP-O's *against* half, as a bound on finding (1), and a
caution for any reader who would take the paper's categories as chord identities. *What it is:* §2.7's
own sentence (*"grouping chords according to behaviour rather than sound"*, with the IV⁶/⁴ against V⁶/⁵
example — *"which both tend to proceed to I"*); §2.5's result that second-order context changes nothing on
its datasets and that categorisation *"is primarily dependent on very local structure"*; and §2.3's I⁴
categorised as dominant. **These are the paper's own reasons why its categories are not chord identities
and why a categorisation by continuation cannot stand in for the chord decision L2 owns.** *Bound:* the
second-order result is stated for the paper's datasets and not measured beyond them.

**Finding (6) — ★ A PUBLISHED PROVENANCE STATEMENT FOR ANALYSES THE RECORD SAYS ARE THE ORIGIN OF THE

371 chorales were made: the first 70 with undergraduates and graduate students in a Princeton course, the

undergraduate, and all cross-validated with music21 with discrepancies further analysed.** *What is NOT
established:* **that dataset 12/13's analyses and the When-in-Rome Bach chorale files are the same
analyses** — the paper names *When in Rome* nowhere in the 26 pages as read (a reader's negative; that

D-474 block already names for the Mozart sonatas and BCMH (*"consensus-built, so agreement cannot be

absence finding changes.** *Applied nowhere; put to the user as a question with its two halves marked.*

**Finding (7) — The slice as the atomic unit, in another published pipeline.** *Candidate for:* the
ground under **D-023** (*"The atomic analysis unit is the constant-sonority slice, never the metric beat"*,

**Finding (8) — The reference-list result** — at §8.

**Finding (9) — A comparability fact for the question row 25 left with the user and row 65 extended.**
*Candidate for:* the comparability question standing with the user (the progress record's row-25 block;

## 4. What the record's decision points take from this paper, and what they do not — answered at the object

**No ratified text names this paper** (§6). So nothing in `FRAMEWORK.md` rests on it, and this section
places the paper against the decision points it bears on so that a later reader can see where it would
enter, not where it has.

**DP-B (tonality first, then chord? CHOSEN: no) and DP-E (tonality decided with the chords; a change
located at a harmonic boundary).** The paper decides tonality, chord and function TOGETHER in one dynamic
programme over the windowed graph, and locates a tonality change only where a cadence in the new tonality
is found. That is an instance of DP-B's chosen side and DP-E's, published in 2007 with hand-set weights and
NO measurement of the joint-versus-separate cost. It adds no figure to DP-B's ground (the measured
5-point and 2-point cost is another paper's) and it contradicts nothing. **What it adds is a worked
shape:** the tonality candidates are pre-filtered per window by an accidental test before the decode
(§2.3), so the joint decision runs over a tonality set already pruned by a hard diatonicity rule — a
pruning the record's own C36 argument (§4.2, *"a tonality model rating candidates by those tones rates
the true tonality lowest exactly where it is most strongly prolonged"*) does not touch, because the
paper's filter is a feasibility cut and not a rating.

**DP-C (segmentation before, with, or after chord identity? CHOSEN: with).** The paper is an instance of
DP-C's *"before (published; every fixed grid)"* rival: the bar is cut into windows at the shortest figure
duration before any harmonic decision, and the authors report the cost in their own words — chords
*"split by the windowing process"* that must be *"merged again"*, work they describe as ongoing. **It is
a published statement, by a system's own authors, that a fixed grid produces boundaries the harmony does
not have.** It carries no figure.

**DP-D (where does the chord-tone assignment live? CHOSEN: part of L2's one decision).** The paper's
melodic analysis is DP-D's excluded rival, *"an input, from an elaboration detector running first"* — with
one difference DP-D's candidate list does not describe: the detector runs first but leaves its CONFLICTS
undecided, and those are settled after the harmonic decision by membership in the decided chord (§2.6).
So the shape is *first-running detector with a post-decision resolution of its own ambiguities*. DP-D's
ground for exclusion — *"a first-running detector's mistakes are unrecoverable downstream"* — reaches
this shape for every note the detector tagged without conflict, whatever its confidence label, and does
not reach the notes it left in conflict. The paper reports no figure for its tagger (the F .72 at DP-D is another paper's). **Finding
(4) records this as an addition candidate to DP-D's rival record: a sub-shape, not a new candidate.**

**DP-I (cadence a layer, and on which side? CHOSEN: split — cues at L1, type at L3).** In the paper the
cadence is neither: it is INSIDE the joint decision, as the edge weights that make D→T progressions
dominate the path score and as the only licence for a tonality change. Table 4's cadence types are read
off the decided degrees, but their weight is applied during the decode. This is a third shape beside
DP-I's two rivals, *wholly upstream* and *wholly downstream*: cadence as a term of the joint objective.
The record's own §4.3 move 3 reads cadences off the decision and never revises it; the paper's cadence
both shapes the decision and is read off it. **No figure supports either side; it is recorded as a shape.**

**DP-K (what is published where it cannot decide? CHOSEN: rivals with mass).** The paper publishes one
best path and no rivals, with per-note confidence labels on the melodic tags only. An instance of
DP-K's excluded rival for the harmonic decision.

**DP-L (chord symbol a derivation? CHOSEN: yes).** Consistent: the chord is a set of note names decided
in the decode; no symbol is decided.

**DP-O (hierarchical reading? NONE CHOSEN).** **This paper is not evidence on DP-O's question as DP-O
states it.** It builds a
layered graph, not a tree; its edges connect successive windows only; no chord functions in two
tonalities at once; no grammar, no parse, no recursion. Its placement in the grammar group of the
proposed order (§0) is not a claim about its method and this read finds no ground for one. **DP-O stays
NONE CHOSEN and this row moves it nowhere.**

**DP-P (how are the terms of L2's score combined and fitted? NOT DECIDED HERE).** The paper's combination
is a sum of hand-set edge weights along a path, *"established empirically"*, with no procedure stated,
no held-out data and no fit — and its authors name learning the weights from a tagged corpus as future
work. It is the pre-fitting end of DP-P's question: a worked example of what the weights look like when
no one fits them (a D→T cadence at 1500–2500 against a T→S at 75), and of a design that carries its own
authors' statement that this is provisional.

**§4.2's entanglement (four questions, one decision).** The paper settles tonality, chord and function
together, and the chord-tone assignment HALF-together (§2.6). It does not settle the boundary with them:
the boundary is the fixed grid. So of the record's four entangled questions it takes three into one
decision and leaves one outside, and its own discussion reports the cost of leaving that one outside.

**D-335 (the function layer outputs the Roman numeral; T/S/D is a derived read-out, never a stored
output) and the D-586 paragraph.** The paper does the opposite of D-335: the tonal function is a NODE
LABEL decided in the decode, the degree is read off the chord's root, and Table 3's degree→function map
is many-valued (III → S, T, D), so the function is a decision and not a derivation there. This is the rival
D-335 excludes, with its ground at §2.4: the many-valued map is why the paper needs the decode to pick
the function. **Recorded beside D-335 as the published rival shape; applied nowhere.**

**D-337 (a lean toward another degree is a tonicization by default; a key change needs a confirming
cadence AND persistence).** The paper's *"tonality changes are allowed only when a cadence in a new
tonality is found"* is D-337's cadence half without its persistence half — and the authors report the
consequence: modulation points displaced by ±one chord, which they attribute to the dynamic programme.
**A published instance of the cadence-only rule and its stated cost.** Recorded beside D-337; applied
nowhere.

**D-527 (no live non-chord-tone cleaning stage; each tone emitted by category inside the one decode).**
The paper has the cleaning stage D-527 forbids, running first, rule-based, with a confidence per note.
The rival, published; no figure.

**D-023 (the atomic unit is the constant-sonority slice, never the metric beat).** The paper's unit is a
per-bar window at the shortest notated duration in that bar — neither the beat nor the slice: a grid the
paper presents as fine enough to hold every voice's notes, which coincides with the slice boundaries
wherever a change point falls on the grid, and which the authors' own compaction remark shows to cut
where the sonority does not change. Whether an onset can fall off that grid (a tuplet, say) is not
addressed by the paper and not derived here. A third unit beside D-023's two.

## 2. The input, the output and the repertoire, established at the object

**The input of chapters 3 to 5 is a CHORD SYMBOL SEQUENCE from a jazz lead sheet, already segmented by
a human.** Table 4.1 (printed 75) gives the stored fields per chord: **Root** (integer pitch class
0–11, relative to the main tonality), **Type** (a tetrad symbol from a small vocabulary, e.g. '', 'm',
'M7'), **Additions** (further transcribed tones, optional), **Bass** (pitch class, optional), and
**Duration** (in pulses). **Enharmonic spelling is deliberately excluded** (printed 75): the author
states two reasons — that spelling in jazz lead sheets is unreliable and chosen for ease of reading,
and that spelling is treated as a problem the analysis should solve rather than a constraint on it.
Footnote 1 (printed 74) records that **time signature and tonality are stored but "do not play a role
in any of the models described in this thesis"**.

**The input of chapter 6 is note-level MIDI**, keyboard notes in a symbolic electronic format (printed
130), with **an annotation of the input marking where a small metric unit occurs** — half bars here —
which printed 151 says must be supplied and is not inferred.

**The output is a PATH THROUGH LONGUET-HIGGINS'S TWO-DIMENSIONAL TONAL SPACE**, expressed as a list of
two-dimensional coordinates, one per chord, together with a cadential function per movement —
authentic (dominant), plagal (subdominant), or a movement following a tonic chord (printed 122). The
semantics is a list of tonic passages and resolved cadences (printed 53). **The output is NOT a
tonality label, NOT a Roman numeral, NOT a chord identity, NOT an inversion, NOT a bass, and NOT a
segmentation** — for chapters 3 to 5 the segmentation is the human's, given in the input. Chapter 6's
system does segment, and that is what forces a new comparison method (§3, §5).

**The repertoire is JAZZ.** The corpus is the author's own: **76 chord sequences, 3,084 chords** (Table
4.4, printed 88), mean length 40.6, shortest 6, longest 93 — jazz standards from lead sheets, filtered
to those the grammar can parse. **Sequences the lexicon could not analyse were excluded from the
dataset entirely** (printed 87–88), and the author names Thelonious Monk's *Epistrophy* as an example
of a piece considered to fall outside the grammar's intended domain. **The dataset is stated to be
available at `http://jazzparser.granroth-wilding.co.uk/JazzCorpus` (printed 74); it was not fetched.**

**THIS PROJECT'S OWN REPERTOIRE APPEARS TWICE, IN ILLUSTRATIONS AND IN NO EXPERIMENT.** *(i)* Example
2.6 (printed 40–42) is a **tonal-space analysis of the opening twelve bars of J. S. Bach's Prelude
No. 1 from the *Eight Short Preludes and Fugues*, BWV 553**, with the engraved passage reproduced, the
path labelled by bar and pulse, and the author's prose reading of it; printed 40 records that the
analysis was **previously presented in Wilding (2008)**, the author's own Master's thesis. *(ii)*
Figure 3.7 (printed 70) is a harmonic analysis of the opening of Bach's *Ermuntre Dich, mein schwacher
Geist*, **simplified from Rohrmeier (2011)** — reproduced to show a structure the thesis's own grammar
does NOT handle. **Neither is part of any experiment, neither is measured, and no Bach music enters
the corpus.** *(★ CORRECTED at this extract's own whole reading, §11 defect (b). **FORMER WORDING,
PRESERVED (#12):** "**One page of this project's own repertoire appears and is not part of any
experiment.** Figure 3.7 (printed 70) is a harmonic analysis of the first two bars of Bach's *Ermuntre
Dich, mein schwacher Geist*, **simplified from Rohrmeier (2011) figure 3** — reproduced to show a
structure the thesis's own grammar does not handle. It is an illustration of a rival's analysis, not a
measurement." **It named one appearance where there are two, gave a bar count for the second that the
page does not state, and attributed a figure number to Rohrmeier (2011) that this side did not read at

## 4. What this project's decision points take from it, and what they do not

Every claim here is against `FRAMEWORK.md` read at the object this sitting — §4.2 (lines 237–271) and
the whole design-point section, DP-A through DP-Q (lines 669–815).

**DP-O — "Does the framework commit to a hierarchical reading of harmony?" NONE CHOSEN. This is the
row's centre of gravity, and it moves the evidence without settling the point.** DP-O's falsifier is
stated at line 798: *"a tree model beating a matched-capacity sequence model on this repertoire's
ground truth, measured on the same corpus and the same axis."* Against that shape, the thesis's Table
5.2:

- **Same corpus — MET.** All models are trained and tested on the one jazz corpus with 10-fold
  cross-validation.
- **Same axis — MET.** All are compared on the tonal space edit distance, and the two grammar models
  additionally on dependency recovery.
- **Tree ahead of sequence — MET, and by a wider margin than row 65's paper reports.** PCCG's
  f-measure 90.50 and ST+PCCG's 91.46 against HmmPath's 80.98.
- **Statistically tested — MET, which row 65's paper did not do.** Bikel's stratified shuffling test
  with 100,000 shuffles, significance below p = 0.05; the results marked bold in Table 5.2 are the ones
  significantly different from the baseline.
- **Matched capacity — NOT met.** No parameter count, no capacity budget and no matched-size
  comparison appears anywhere in the thesis as read.
- **This repertoire's ground truth — NOT met.** Jazz chord symbols and one annotator's tonal-space
  paths; no Roman numeral, no key label, no Baroque or classical music in any experiment.
- **And one clause DP-O's wording does not name, which this thesis supplies against itself:** by §3.5
  the grammar is **not hierarchical in the sense DP-O's "for" half describes**. DP-O's *for* sentence
  is about *"the same surface chords functioning simultaneously as a tonic phrase in one tonality and a
  dominant phrase in another"* — and printed 70–71 says in terms that this is the structure the present
  thesis ignores. **So the thesis is a derivation-tree model whose SEMANTICS is a flat list of tonic
  passages and cadences.** Calling it a tree model beating a sequence model is true of its derivations
  and misleading about its analyses, and the distinction is the author's own.

**DP-O therefore stays NONE CHOSEN, and nothing here is proposed on.**

**DP-C — "Is segmentation decided before, with, or after chord identity?" CHOSEN: with.** Chapter 6 is
a **published instance of the chosen side at the note level**, and it carries a consequence the record
does not yet hold: **when segmentation is inside the decision, the comparison method itself has to
change.** Printed 140: *"Because the parser incorporates the task of chord segmentation, it is not
possible to evaluate its DR directly against the gold standard. This same problem exists for evaluation
of any system that performs segmentation of its input as a part of the analysis process."* The remedy —
an alignment-maximising comparison with a stated one-sided bias, quantified at printed 147 — is a worked
shape for a measurement question this project owns.

**DP-K — "What does the analysis publish where it cannot decide?" CHOSEN: rivals in the same stream,
each with its mass.** The thesis publishes **one best analysis** and, where the grammar admits none, no
analysis at all — reported as a **coverage** figure beside the accuracy (Table 5.2: PCCG 97.37,
ST+PCCG 100, HmmPath 100). It is therefore **a published instance of the rival DP-K excludes**, with
its own failure mode visible: printed 120 proposes a backoff to the baseline model precisely so the
system always returns something. **Recorded as a rival's worked shape; DP-K is not reopened.**

**DP-Q — "May the analysis decline to read a span at all?" NONE CHOSEN — underived, open.** The thesis
gives the question a shape the record does not yet carry: **its system declines not by judgment but by
grammatical failure**, and the author's answer is a backoff model that never declines, chosen so that
coverage is total. Printed 120 states the cost plainly — the backoff analyses *"will in general be of
poorer quality than the parser's output"*. **That is a third position beside DP-Q's two — decline, or
answer badly and say which — and it is recorded, not proposed on.**

**DP-A — "Divide the deciding by published field?" CHOSEN: no.** The thesis does not divide by
published field: one derivation carries the tonal relation and the cadential function together. It is
consistent with the chosen side and adds no measurement to it, because it never separates the fields
to compare.

**DP-B and DP-E — tonality decided with the chords.** Chapters 3 to 5 do not decide a tonality at all:
the output is a path of relations, and printed 49 states that *"absolute position in the space is
meaningless"*. **This is a fourth possibility beside DP-B's two, and it is worth naming exactly: not
"tonality first", not "tonality with the chords", but tonality NEVER NAMED — only the relations
between chords published, with the starting point arbitrary.** Whether that is available to this
project is settled elsewhere and not here: the output this analysis must produce writes a tonality
attached to a chord (§4.2's fourth bullet, `FRAMEWORK.md` lines 259–262). **Recorded as an excluded
shape with the ground for excluding it already in the record.**

**DP-D — "Where does the chord-tone assignment live?" CHOSEN: part of L2's one decision.** The thesis
has **no chord-tone assignment at all** in chapters 3 to 5, its input being chord symbols. Chapter 6's
chord recogniser assumes conditional independence of notes given a chord label — the **bag-of-notes**
assumption — and printed 150 names it, with the projection onto pitch classes, as **one of the two
biggest problems with the proposed model**, citing Raphael & Stoddard (candidacy row 2) for both the
assumption and the objection to it. **That is a rival's own author reporting the defect DP-D's chosen
side avoids, and it adds no new candidate to DP-D's list.**

**DP-I — "Is cadence a layer, and on which side?" CHOSEN: split — cues at L1, type at L3.** In the
thesis cadence is neither: **it is the grammar's central semantic object**, the thing the logical forms
denote. Row 34's extract records a third shape beside DP-I's two (cadence as a term of the joint
objective); **this is a fourth — cadence as the representation itself**, with no separate detector and
no separate label. Recorded.

**D-023 — the atomic analysis unit.** The thesis's unit in chapters 3 to 5 is **the human-supplied
chord symbol**; in chapter 6 it is a segment the chord recogniser proposes over a half-bar grid the
input must be annotated with. Neither is the constant-sonority slice.

**Where the record does NOT reach it.** `FRAMEWORK.md` names this thesis **nowhere** — not by name, not
by any characterisation term run, not by any figure (§6). Neither does `CLAUDE.md`, `DECISIONS.md`,
`STATUS.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `OPEN_ITEMS.md`, `decisions/group_A.md`, `reading_pass/population.md`
or the findings surface. **No ratified text of this project rests on it.**

## 5. What the thesis reports, and what each number is a number OF

**Table 5.1 (printed 107) — supertagging models compared, chord input.** BestNgram (the bigram model,
no low-count cutoff, Witten-Bell smoothing) entropy 1.13, accuracy 77.11 %; CANDC (the C&C linguistic
supertagger used off the shelf) entropy 1.39, accuracy 80.22 %. **Each number is a number OF** the
model's top-ranked category against the annotator's own category choice, pooled over ten folds. The
author notes CANDC was used *"only with its default settings"*.

**Table 5.2 (printed 125) — the chord-input result, and the table this row exists for.** As printed,
precision / recall / f-measure for tonal space edit distance (TSED) and for dependency recovery (DR),
then coverage, all percentages; **bold marks a significant improvement over the baseline**:

| Model | TSED P | TSED R | TSED F | DR P | DR R | DR F | Cov. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HmmPath | 77.44 | 84.87 | 80.98 | — | — | — | 100 |
| PCCG | **92.29** | 88.78 | **90.50** | 90.25 | 86.83 | 88.51 | 97.37 |
| ST+PCCG | **90.18** | **92.79** | **91.46** | 88.22 | 90.78 | 89.48 | 100 |

**What each number is a number OF:** agreement between the model's single highest-probability analysis
and **the author's own annotation of the same 76 sequences**, pooled over ten cross-validation folds —
TSED by the closeness of the interpretation as a path through the tonal space, DR by the accuracy of
the tonal relations read as a dependency graph. **Coverage** is the share of sequences for which the
model returned any analysis; PCCG's 97.37 is two parse failures, which printed 126 says were one
timeout and one beam loss.

**Table 5.3 (printed 126) — average CPU time per sequence:** HmmPath 0:03 (standard deviation 0:01),
PCCG 34:17 (75:23), ST+PCCG 9:22 (33:32), each on a 2.6 GHz AMD Opteron 6212.

**Table 6.1 (printed 147) — how much the new comparison method flatters.** On the chord-input result,
where the true alignment is known, ST+PCCG measures DR 88.22 / 90.78 / 89.48 and ODR 89.65 / 92.25 /
90.93. **So ODR overestimates by roughly one to one-and-a-half points on this system** — the author's
words are *"by only a couple of percentage points on each measure"* — and printed 147 adds that ODR
becomes more generous the worse the system is, so the bias is larger where the result is lower.

**Table 6.2 (printed 148) — the MIDI result.** ST+PCCG repeated from Table 5.2 as a **ceiling, not a
baseline** (printed 147, in those words, because it is a result from an easier task):

| Model | TSED P | TSED R | TSED F | ODR P | ODR R | ODR F | Cov |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ST+PCCG | 90.18 | 92.79 | 91.46 | 89.65 | 92.25 | 90.93 | 100 |
| CR+HmmPath, pipeline | 42.14 | 46.15 | 44.06 | — | — | — | 100 |
| CR+HmmPath, lattice | 40.22 | 44.39 | 42.21 | — | — | — | 100 |
| CR+ST+PCCG, pipeline | 61.77 | **55.93** | **58.71** | 58.04 | **52.48** | **55.12** | 92.68 |
| CR+ST+PCCG, lattice | **64.17** | 47.98 | 54.90 | **61.03** | 45.63 | 52.22 | 90.24 |

**Bold is significantly higher than all other systems excluding the chord-sequence parser**, by the
same stratified shuffling test. The author's own reading, printed 149: *"the accuracy of the parser's
output is still low. These results should be seen more as a proof of concept."*

**Table 4.5 (printed 89) — the annotator-consistency experiment, and the paragraph that bounds it.**
Ten sequences chosen at random, 386 chords, **reannotated by the same annotator about two years later
without reference to the original annotations**:

| Metric | Precision | Recall | F-score |
|---|---|---|---|
| TSED | 99.07 | 98.76 | 98.91 |
| DR | 99.38 | 99.69 | 99.53 |
| AA | 98.16 | 98.16 | 98.16 |

*(AA is the thesis's own third metric, expanded in its Table of Acronyms as **"anotation accuracy"** —

**What these numbers are numbers OF:** the similarity of one annotator's second reading to that same

## 7. The findings, each with what it is a candidate for and what bounds it

**(1) THE THESIS SUPERSEDES ROW 65's NUMBERS FOR THE SAME EXPERIMENTS, BY THE AUTHOR'S OWN STATEMENT,
AND ONE DIRECTION FLIPS.** Footnote 7 (printed 125): *"Granroth-Wilding & Steedman (2012b) reported a
slightly different set of results from the same experiments carried out with a subtly different model
and different beam parameters. The experiments reported here match more closely the experiments of
Hockenmaier (2003) and use the beam settings determined in section 5.3.4.4."* Read against row 65's
extract §5, which prints that paper's Table 1 as HmmPath 84.3 f-measure, PCCG 80.6, St+PCCG 88.3,
St+PCCG+HmmPath 88.7: **the grammar without the supertagger moves from 80.6, BELOW the baseline, to
90.50, well ABOVE it and marked significant.** *What it is a candidate for:* a correction to row 65's
extract's finding (1), which carries *"the paper's own Table 1 showing the grammar WITHOUT the
supertagger BELOW the baseline (F 80.6)"* as a bound on the falsifier-shape claim — **that bound does
not survive the author's later report of the same experiments.** *What bounds it:* the thesis states
the models differ subtly and the beam settings differ; it does not say which report is to be preferred,
and neither does this read. **Two reports of one experiment, and the record now holds both.**

**(2) THE SIGNIFICANCE TEST ROW 65's PAPER LACKED IS PRESENT HERE, NAMED AND PARAMETERISED.** Bikel's
stratified shuffling test, 100,000 random shuffles, significance below p = 0.05, with the significant
cells marked bold and the non-significant differences stated in prose — printed 125 says in terms that
the difference between PCCG's and ST+PCCG's f-measures is **not** significant on either metric. *What
it is a candidate for:* row 65's extract records under principle #24 that *"whether that gap clears the
fold-to-fold spread is not derivable from the paper"*. **At this object it is derivable, and it
clears** — for the grammar-against-baseline comparison. *What bounds it:* the test is significance, not
spread; no confidence interval is printed anywhere, so the SIZE of any gap still carries no stated
uncertainty, and #24's demand is met on one axis and not the other.

**(3) THE THESIS'S GRAMMAR IS EXPLICITLY NOT HIERARCHICAL IN THE SENSE DP-O's "FOR" HALF DESCRIBES, AND
THE AUTHOR SAYS SO.** §3.5 and printed 70–71, quoted at §3 above. *What it is a candidate for:* a
qualification on any reading of rows 65 and 66 as evidence for DP-O — **their derivations are trees;
their analyses are flat sequences of tonic passages and cadences, and the recursive key structure
DP-O's *for* sentence names is named by this author as out of scope.** *What bounds it:* it is a
statement about this thesis's grammar and about no other; row 21's and row 22's grammars are not
touched by it, and this read did not re-open either extract for comparison.

**(4) A MEASURED INTRA-ANNOTATOR CONSISTENCY FIGURE, WITH INTER-ANNOTATOR AGREEMENT DECLARED
UNMEASURED BY THE AUTHOR.** Table 4.5 and the two quoted passages at §5. *What it is a candidate for:*
principle #21 and `OPEN_ITEMS.md` OI-179. The record's D-474 establishes a FACT-of-absence for
**published per-axis inter-annotator agreement on Roman-numeral or key annotation of Baroque/classical
symbolic music**. **This does not contradict it and must not be read as doing so**: the repertoire is
jazz, the axis is a tonal-space path with cadential function, and the quantity measured is one
annotator's self-consistency. **What it does supply is a worked instance of the practice #21 demands
being carried out on a corpus of this literature, with the two quantities kept apart and the missing
one declared rather than glossed** — which is the shape OI-179's own design surface has to choose
between. *What bounds it:* ten sequences and 386 chords out of 76 and 3,084; a single annotator who is
the author; a two-year gap the author himself says cannot entirely rule out memory of the first pass;
and an axis this project does not measure on.

**(5) THE CONSISTENCY CEILING SITS ABOVE THE SYSTEM HERE — THE OPPOSITE SIGN TO DP-K's POPULAR-MUSIC
GROUND, ON A THIRD DOMAIN AND A DIFFERENT QUANTITY.** The annotator's self-consistency is 98.91 TSED
f-measure and 99.53 DR f-measure; the best system reaches 91.46 and 89.48 on the same metrics and the
same corpus. `FRAMEWORK.md` DP-K (lines 734–740) rests partly on *"one study of popular-music audio in
which the automatic systems it evaluated scored about ten percent above the annotator-pairwise
agreement that same study measured"*, with a second study of the same domain reporting the opposite
sign recorded beside it and **no contradiction asserted between them**. *What it is a candidate for:* a
third datum for that ground, on symbolic jazz. *What bounds it, and it is the bound that matters:*
**DP-K's ground is about annotator-PAIRWISE agreement and this is one annotator against himself** —
they are not the same quantity, and a self-consistency figure is expected to sit above an agreement
figure for structural reasons. **NO contradiction is asserted, and this must not be merged into DP-K's
ground as a third study of the same thing.** Recorded beside it, exactly as the record already handles
the two studies it holds.

**(6) SEGMENTATION INSIDE THE DECISION FORCES THE COMPARISON METHOD TO CHANGE, AND THE THESIS
QUANTIFIES ITS OWN REMEDY'S BIAS.** Printed 140, 141, 146, 147. *What it is a candidate for:* DP-C is
CHOSEN with, and this project's L2 decides boundaries with the labelling — **so the measurement-design
phase inherits exactly the problem this chapter names, and a published system has both stated it in
general terms ("this same problem exists for evaluation of any system that performs segmentation of its
input as a part of the analysis process") and measured its own workaround's one-sided bias against a
case where the true alignment is known.** *What bounds it:* the bias was measured on ONE system on
chord input, and printed 147 says the overestimate grows as results fall, so the number does not
transfer.

**(7) A PUBLISHED SYSTEM THAT CAN FAIL TO PRODUCE ANY READING, AND ITS AUTHOR'S ANSWER.** Coverage is a
reported column; parse failure is a real outcome; §5.3.6 (printed 120) proposes backing off to the
baseline model so coverage is total, and states the cost — poorer analyses — rather than hiding it.
*What it is a candidate for:* DP-Q, which is NONE CHOSEN and asks whether *no confident reading* and
*no chord here* are the same publication. **This is a third thing again: no GRAMMATICAL reading, which
is neither.** *What bounds it:* the thesis does not frame it as DP-Q's question and takes no position
on abstention as a judgment.

**(8) A LEXICON WHOSE COVERAGE THE AUTHOR ARGUES CANNOT BE FIXED BY ENUMERATION.** Printed 87: the
frequency of lexical categories over the corpus follows a roughly Zipfian distribution (Figure 4.2), and
*"it would, therefore, be futile to attempt to achieve a high coverage of jazz standards by adding new
categories to the lexicon for each rare substitution encountered."* Printed 120 repeats it for the
statistical models: as the lexicon grows, exponentially more training data is needed. *What it is a
candidate for:* the candidate-admission question this project's record already carries — the argument
is that a hand-enumerated vocabulary of chord readings has a long tail that enumeration cannot close.
*What bounds it:* measured on jazz chord symbols with this lexicon and this corpus; the thesis offers
no measurement of what a different vocabulary would do, and names lexicon learning as unexplored.

**(9) THE CORPUS EXCLUDES WHAT THE GRAMMAR CANNOT PARSE, AND THE AUTHOR STATES WHAT THAT DOES TO THE
NUMBERS.** Printed 88 says sequences that could not be fully analysed were excluded from the dataset
entirely; printed 126 draws the consequence: *"The corpus used here for training and evaluation
includes only sequences to which it was possible to assign a harmonic interpretation using the grammar.
The results reported for the models that use the grammar are, therefore, higher than would be expected
on real-life chord sequences."* *What it is a candidate for:* the same bound row 65's extract already
carries as *"the paper's own bound that the filtered corpus inflates the grammar's figures"* — **here it
is stated by the author in a fuller form and applies to Table 5.2 as well.** *What bounds it:* the
author gives no estimate of the size of the inflation.

**(10) NO HELD-OUT TEST SET ANYWHERE, STATED BY THE AUTHOR AS A LIMITATION AND NOT AS A DETAIL.**
Printed 76: *"Due to its small size, the jazz corpus contains no heldout test set or development set"*,
and *"whilst this reduces the problem of over-fitting models to their training data, it is not a
satisfactory alternative to using completely unseen test data."* Printed 77 is sharper: the
supertagger's parameters were chosen by cross-validation over the same corpus used to evaluate the
parser that uses it, so *"The results from cross-validation should be thought of as a preliminary
evaluation on a development set."* *What it is a candidate for:* principle #20's separation of fitting
from evaluation — this is a published system whose author declares the separation not achieved and says
which way the resulting bias runs. *What bounds it:* it is the author's declaration, not a measurement
of the bias.

**(11) THE NOTE-LEVEL MODEL ROW 65's EXTRACT SAID TO LOOK FOR EXISTS, AND IT IS CHAPTER 6.** Row 65's
page 8 named a note-level successor as future work; row 65's extract's finding (4) made *"the first
question row 66's reader asks of the thesis"* whether the thesis contains that paper's experiment,
extends it, or delivers the note-level input. **The answer, at the object: all three.** Chapter 5 is
that experiment, re-run with a subtly different model and different beam parameters (finding 1);
chapter 6 delivers the note-level input, as a proof of concept whose accuracy the author calls low; and
printed 130 records that some of chapter 6 was published as Granroth-Wilding & Steedman (2012a), a
separate work not held here. *What bounds it:* nothing about that 2012a paper is established — it was
not opened.

**(12) ONE CHORD CARRYING TWO FUNCTIONS AT ONCE, WORKED AT A CASE AND SAID TO BE UNREPRESENTABLE IN
THIS THESIS'S OWN TREES.** Printed 43, on a passage of *Autumn Leaves* shown in figure 2.10 under two
derivations: the Em⁷ can be heard as the tonic ending one cadence or as an extended dominant beginning
the next, and *"A third, and perhaps more plausible, way of viewing the connection between the Em⁷ and
the E♭⁷ in this latter analysis is to treat the Em⁷ as having two functions: a tonic at the right edge
of the first subtree of figure 2.10a and a dominant at the left edge of the second. Such double
functions are represented in the analyses of Rohrmeier (2011)."* The author then says the phenomenon
matters: *"Such ambiguities, featuring multiple plausible alternative readings, are common in music
and it is essential to a theory of harmonic structure that it be capable of explaining precisely the
differences between the alternative readings."* *What it is a candidate for:* it sharpens finding (3)
at a worked case — **the structure this grammar cannot represent is not only hierarchical modulation
but a single chord holding two functions**, and the author names a rival (candidacy row 22) whose
formalism does represent it. It also sits beside DP-K's first added ground, that *"at every moment a
score can carry two defensible key labels at once"* — **the same shape one axis down, on chord
function rather than tonality.** *What bounds it, and the bound is firm:* this is an author's worked
illustration on one jazz passage, **not a measurement, not a corpus statistic, and not on this
repertoire.** DP-K's ground stands on its own sources and gains nothing measurable here; **no figure of
this thesis is offered for it and none is merged into it.**

**(13) THE THESIS CHARACTERISES ROW 34 AT A PRIMARY, AND ITS CHARACTERISATION AGREES WITH ROW 34's OWN
EXTRACT.** Printed 20: *"Illescas et al. (2007) present a graph-based computational model of harmonic
analysis based on the Riemannian notion of chord function and also exploiting regularities in the
transitions between consecutive chords."* — placed in a paragraph about hidden Markov and related
models, which the author then bounds: *"they fall short as a model of musical cognition, since they
are unable to capture any long-distance relationships in the underlying structures ... An HMM is only
able to capture dependencies between adjacent structural elements and, where non-adjacent
relationships exist, they are treated as noise."* *What it is a candidate for:* row 34 was read at the
object the sitting before this one, and its extract describes a dynamic programme over a window-layered
graph deciding chord, tonality, degree and function together. **A separate author's characterisation,
published in 2013, agrees on the two properties row 34's extract names as central —
graph-based and transition-exploiting — and adds the criticism that such a model cannot carry
long-distance structure.** *What bounds it:* it is one sentence of a literature review, written by an
author with a stake in the contrary position; it measures nothing about row 34's system, and **it is
recorded as a citation agreeing with the record, never as evidence about row 34's accuracy.**

## 10. Verdict

**NOT CENTRAL.**

*Why not central.* The record names this thesis in no ratified text and in no derived artifact of the
staged tree (§6). It decides none of L2's publications: its output is a path of tonal relations with a
cadential function per movement, and it names no tonality, no Roman numeral, no chord identity, no
inversion and no bass. Its ground truth is one annotator's reading of jazz lead sheets on an axis this
project does not measure on. Its numbers carry a named significance test but no spread. Its lexicon is
hand-built and designed for one genre, and its corpus is filtered to what that lexicon can parse — a
filter the author says inflates the grammar models' results. **The author's own claim about the
lexicon's reach is carried whole rather than in the half that supports the verdict** (printed 46):
*"Whilst the grammar presented here is designed to interpret a particular musical genre, much of it
could equally be applied to the analysis of other tonal harmonic genres. Adapting the grammar to
another genre would primarily involve modifications to the lexicon to add chord substitutions common
in that genre and to remove some specific to jazz that are not used in that genre."* **That is a
statement of intent and carries no measurement on any other genre**, which is why it does not move the
verdict — but the verdict does not rest on a claim of genre-lock the author does not make. *(★
CORRECTED at this extract's own whole reading, §11 defect (e). **FORMER WORDING, PRESERVED (#12):**
"Its lexicon is hand-built and, by its author's own statement, genre-specific". **The author's own
statement is the opposite in its second half, and the sentence quoted only the half that supported the
verdict** — the shape `D-643` forbids of a ruling and this side applies to a source.)*

*The ground on which CENTRAL could be argued, stated in full so the choice is the user's.* **Findings
(1) and (2) together move a bound the record currently carries.** Row 65's extract's finding (1) is the
nearest measured instance of DP-O's falsifier shape this pass has met, and it is recorded with two
weakening bounds: that the grammar without the supertagger fell below the baseline, and that no
significance test was run. **At this object both bounds fail** — the grammar alone is well above the
baseline, and the difference is significant by a named test. If DP-O's open point is the reason the
grammar branch was ruled into the population at all, then the row that strengthens the branch's best
measured instance on two of its recorded weaknesses is arguably central to that point. **Against
that:** the two clauses of the falsifier that decide it — matched capacity and this repertoire's ground
truth — are still not met, and finding (3) adds a third obstacle the record did not previously hold,
namely that this grammar's analyses are not hierarchical in the sense DP-O's *for* half describes.
**On balance the falsifier is not met and DP-O is not moved, which is why the verdict is NOT CENTRAL —
but the bound that was doing the work in row 65's extract is gone, and that is a change to the record's
evidence rather than to its verdict.**

**A second independent extraction is NOT owed unless the user flips the verdict.** *(★ THE WORD `independent` IN THAT SENTENCE IS FLAGGED AND LEFT STANDING, on the user-ordered check of 2026-09-13 that followed this file's landing. It is carried as the record's own name for the procedure, and **this side did not open the commission this sitting**, so that it is the record's term is a relay and not established here. It is left rather than reworded because renaming a procedure the record names would be worse than flagging it. **§11's absolutes sweep struck the same word twice elsewhere in this file and did not reach this use** — see the addition at the foot of §11.)*

## Bearing on the framework — flagged, not decided (verdicts belong to Task 4)

**Read against `FRAMEWORK.md` §9 (DP-O) and §11 (R-7), both read at the file this session.**

**★ R-7's THIRD NAMED UNREAD ALTERNATIVE IS NOW READ.** R-7 names three: *"a tonality estimated at
every window size at once"* (row 17, Sapp — read), *"a time-span reduction tree"* (**this row**), and
*"tonality in a transform space rather than as a discrete label"* (row 18, Wavescapes — read).
**With this chapter, all three are read at a primary.** Whether that discharges R-7 is Task 4's; what
is established is that the reading gap R-7 names is closed.

**DP-O — this row supplies NEITHER support NOR a falsifier, and the reason is sharper than "no
measurement".** DP-O asks whether the framework commits to *a hierarchical reading of harmony*, and
names its falsifier as *a tree model beating a matched-capacity sequence model on this repertoire's
ground truth*. This chapter:

1. **does not model harmony hierarchically at all** — the prolongational reduction, the subtheory that
   *"explicitly indicat[es] harmonic retention and change"*, **is the one it did not implement** (p. 209);
2. **is monophonic**, where this project's repertoire is four-voice chorales;
3. **reports no comparison against any sequence model**, matched-capacity or otherwise;
4. and its trees are **reductions of a melody**, graded against expert GTTM annotations — a different
   object and a different ground truth from DP-O's.

**So DP-O stays open exactly as it was, and this row cannot move it.** *NOT claimed:* that no GTTM-line
paper could bear on DP-O; the prolongational analyzer was *"being developed"* in 2013 and later work in
the line (σGTTM, deepGTTM) is unread here.

**★ WHAT THE ROW DOES CONTRIBUTE, AND IT IS NOT NOTHING — two facts about the shape of the problem.**

- **The dependency direction.** The best-developed time-span-reduction implementation puts its
  hierarchy **downstream of tonality and harmony**, needs region and chord distances to run its most
  consequential grouping rule, and **does not compute them**. Any future proposal that hierarchy should

  results already considered correct, and still reaches **F ≈ 0.49 automatically** on monophonic
  eight-bar excerpts. **That is a measured statement about tractability**, and it is the same shape as
  HarmTrace's parse-space finding (row 5) from a different direction: a rich hierarchical formalism
  becomes runnable by having something taken out of it or bolted onto it.

analyzer scores **0.84 at default parameters**, against grouping's 0.46. Metrical structure is, on this
evidence, much the more mechanically recoverable of the two. Read beside V5's finding that removing
metrical-accent features costs about six points of F-measure in a segmental analyser, it is
consistent — the metrical layer is both recoverable and useful — but **these are different corpora,
different objects and different metrics, and no arithmetic joins them.**

## Bearing — flagged for the user and for any later verdict, NOT decided here

- **★ The mode question** (routed by the disposition surface to the L2 detail specification, the
  measurement design and the style system). **This is the fullest formal seven-mode vocabulary the
  pass has read**, with roles, quality restrictions per mode, and Tonal Harmony stated as a *proper
  subset* of Modal Harmony. **But it classifies GIVEN chord labels against a GIVEN scale; it infers no
  mode from notes**, so it is a vocabulary and a reasoning scheme, not a mode-detection method. It
  sits beside row 6 (a seven-mode functional ontology, likewise inferring nothing from notes), row 9
  (four-mode detection with the tonic given), row 10 (major-minorness as a continuum) and row 11 (the
  DCML standard's two-valued key axis).
- **★ DP-K — and this is the sharpest thing the row contributes.** MHO **publishes multiple readings**
  — ten for a four-chord progression — which is superficially DP-K's shape. **It publishes them with
  no mass, no ranking and no evidence separating them.** That makes it the **third** system in this
  population to publish alternatives without mass, after HarmTrace's rule-order precedence and row 6's
  flat function classes. **Read together they are an existence proof of what "publish the rivals"
  degenerates into when nothing scores them**, and they show that the load in DP-K's chosen wording is
  carried by the clause *"each with its mass"* rather than by the plurality. *Whether that strengthens
  DP-K's record is a verdict, and is not taken here.*
- **L3's phrase and section grouping.** Sectional form recovered from the **chord stream alone** at
  F1 ≈ 0.60, against 0.42 for the only prior symbolic method and 58.09 ± 15.77 for audio
  state-of-the-art. **Pop repertoire, section labels rather than phrase boundaries**, so it does not
  transfer to L3's own object without argument — but it is evidence that sectional structure is
  substantially recoverable from harmony, which is the direction L3's charter takes.
- **DP-J** — untouched: nothing here compares phrase boundaries with harmonic boundaries.
- **§7 data design / DP-L** — the chord-quality-from-intervals inference by OWL reasoning is a third
  independent instance, beside rows 3 and 8, of the field treating the chord label as **derived** from
  a structured description rather than as a primitive.

  chosen and unthreatened or already open.
